documents.abstract: Abstract Industry 5.0 shifts the focus of manufacturing automation toward human well-being, not just efficiency or output. This means task-allocation systems now have to juggle production targets, ergonomic safety, and what the workforce can realistically handle. Here, we introduce what we call the Ergonomics-Aware Human–Robot Task Allocation (EA-HRTA) problem. Picture it as a complex assignment challenge: for every task, we have to consider execution cost, whether the person or robot has the right skills, the workload each can take on, and the total ergonomic strain humans can safely handle. We turn this challenge into a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) model, so it runs on both quantum-annealing machines and gate-model quantum computers. We lay out three key contributions: first, we develop a penalty-based QUBO model and show exactly how to set penalty weights so it actually works. Second, we roll out a complete system where the very same QUBO gets sent both to a D-Wave-style simulated-annealing sampler and to our own lightweight, dependency-free QAOA statevector simulator. Finally, we’ve built and open-sourced a benchmarking suite that lets you see how quantum solutions perform next to a quick, greedy heuristic and a full-scale CBC integer programming baseline.. Across 60 runs spanning problem sizes from 9 to 240 binary variables, quantum annealing maintains a 100% constraint-feasibility rate at every scale tested, matching classical baselines closely on small instances (within 2% of the exact optimum at N = 9) but exhibiting a solution-quality gap that widens to roughly 140% at N = 240 under fixed penalty weights and a fixed annealing schedule. QAOA achieves competitive cost values only at the smallest instance tested (N = 9) and loses feasibility entirely by N = 16, consistent with known near-term gate-model scalability limits. We report a warm-start ablation seeding the annealer with the greedy solution, which does not yield a consistent improvement, and use this negative result to motivate an adaptive-penalty and problem-decomposition research direction. Rather than claiming a present-day quantum advantage, this paper contributes a reusable ergonomics-aware QUBO formulation, a transparent and reproducible benchmark methodology for the human-centric manufacturing community, and an honest empirical map of where current quantum optimization methods stand relative to classical practice at realistic shop-floor problem sizes.

This conceptual paper introduces Represented Present State Distinguished From Situated State, a structural distinction between the conditions that actually hold and a viewpoint’s current representation of those conditions. Either can change while the other remains fixed. Action and projection can therefore proceed from an account that is incomplete or mistaken, while their consequences depend on the situation itself. The account assesses a representation of the present through the evidence and scope supporting its claims. It asks what each instrument, report, inference, or observation establishes, when it was obtained, and which conditions it reaches. No viewpoint requires a complete representation of the situation. The distinction matters where an omitted or mistaken element changes projection, inquiry, or action. A bad outcome alone does not establish a representational error; an accurate account can also be followed by a poor decision or faulty execution. The discussion connects the distinction to Endsley’s account of situation awareness and examines two documented cases. At Three Mile Island in 1979, operators treated a relief valve as closed while it remained open, and their interpretation of the pressurizer level led them to regard the reactor core as covered. On Lubang Island, Hiroo Onoda retained a wartime representation after the war had ended, rejecting contrary reports until his former commander relieved him of duty in 1974. The cases distinguish a mistaken account of an ongoing condition from an account that persists after conditions have changed. Part of the Possibility and Counterfactual Structure series within On Human Modeling, the paper examines who constructs a representation, who can challenge it, and who bears the consequences when it diverges from the situation. Its framework can inform human–AI research on state estimation, user modeling, evidence provenance, and whether systems distinguish changes in their internal accounts from changes in the conditions those accounts describe.

Public-serving institutions (government agencies, courts, health systems, social-welfare bodies, and regulators) are adopting artificial intelligence (AI) to triage caseloads, allocate resources, detect fraud, and personalize services. Because these institutions exercise coercive and distributive authority over citizens who cannot easily exit the relationship, the stakes of getting AI wrong are qualitatively different from those in commercial settings. This paper surveys the advances, challenges, and future directions of responsible AI in the public sector, synthesizing scholarship on AI in government, algorithmic fairness, transparency, and AI ethics with practitioner-facing governance instruments. We first delimit what makes public-serving institutions distinctive: statutory mandates, due-process obligations, and diffuse accountability. We then map the state of the art across four dimensions (use cases, governance and policy instruments, fairness/transparency/accountability practices, and organizational capacity and procurement) and consolidate representative advances in a described table. We argue that the field has matured from principle proliferation toward operational risk management, exemplified by the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the OECD AI Principles, yet a persistent gap remains between high-level commitments and verifiable practice on the ground. Core challenges include bias and equity harms, threats to legitimacy and due process, opacity and contestability, thin institutional capacity, and fragmented accountability. We conclude with a research and practice agenda emphasizing contestable-by-design systems, sociotechnical evaluation, procurement as governance, participatory oversight, and workforce capability. Responsible AI in public service is less a technical property of models than an institutional achievement sustained over time.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Software security education is still insufficiently addressed in many undergraduate computing curricula. Programs often emphasize attack-oriented activities rather than secure design practices, leaving future developers with limited skills to identify and mitigate vulnerabilities. Active learning approaches, such as serious games, offer opportunities to foster engagement and practical understanding of secure development concepts. We aim to design and evaluate RiskGuard , a card-based serious game that supports the teaching of software vulnerabilities and security patterns, investigating its impact on students’ knowledge, intrinsic motivation, and learning experience. We conducted a controlled experiment with 32 undergraduate students from Systems Analysis and Development (SAD) and Information Security (IS) programs. Participants were assigned to either a traditional lecture or a lecture followed by a RiskGuard session. Learning and motivation were assessed using a Knowledge Assessment Questionnaire and the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI), complemented by qualitative feedback. Our results indicate that RiskGuard supported concept reinforcement and increased students’ engagement and intrinsic motivation, although it did not outperform lecture-only instruction in immediate knowledge-assessment scores. RiskGuard shows potential as a complementary educational tool for promoting secure software design through game-based learning. This study contributes (i) the design and open resources of RiskGuard , (ii) empirical evidence on its learning and motivational effects, and (iii) insights for integrating serious games into cybersecurity and software engineering education.

Experimental laboratory work involves repetitive, labour-intensive manual procedures and strict safety protocols, making it an attractive area for Robotics and Artificial Intelligence (RAI). With research currently focused on technical innovation, there has been little work investigating the human factors of chemist-robot collaboration, and how these technologies will change the nature of work in chemistry. Understanding chemists’ requirements and perspectives is vital to the successful deployment and acceptance of RAI in laboratories. We examined the potential for robot-assisted chemistry experimentation through the perspective of future users by conducting contextual inquiries and semi-structured interviews with nine experimental chemists at various career levels with and without laboratory automation experience. Reflexive thematic analysis was used to gain a situated understanding of how their work could benefit from automation, as well as their perspectives and opinions on working alongside robots. We found that our participants are open to robot-assisted experimentation and have clear ideas for human-robot partnerships in the lab. We identified eight themes characterising chemists’ desired applications, the implementation requirements, and the perspectives on the adoption of robot-assisted experimentation. These findings show that successful acceptance of robot-assisted experimentation depends not only on technical innovation, but also on addressing the practical barriers and concerns of the chemists who will work alongside these systems. The key concern being that RAI should not constrain, but rather complement the role of the chemist in knowledge discovery. The findings contribute to a set of initial design considerations covering hardware, software, and interaction design for successful integration of RAI in experimental laboratory work.

Abstract Background: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to access organisational documentation, including standard operating procedures (SOPs), HR policies and institutional guidelines. However, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approaches that rely on free-form rewriting can introduce hallucinations and unstable trade-offs between completeness and conciseness, particularly in safety-and compliance-critical settings. Objectives: To evaluate extraction as a hallucination-resistant alternative to rewriting-based RAG, and to compare strategies that balance precision, recall and safety across document types and model scales. Methods: We compare multiple prompting strategies, including line-number-based source selection, extraction of relevant guideline sentences with explicit annotation of safety-related content, and a multi-stage pipeline that refines draft answers using supporting evidence from the source guideline. Constrained extraction strategies enable more reliable selection of clinically relevant source content, while direct verbatim copying provides a strong precision-oriented baseline. Experiments are conducted on documents of varying length (local NHS guidelines in acute care and oncology, as well as UK-wide NICE guidelines) and structures, using both frontier-scale and smaller locally deployable models. Performance is assessed using automatic metrics and via human expert evaluation of relevance and completeness. Results: Line-number selection provides the most consistent recall improvements for shorter, protocol-like guidelines across both large and small models, achieving medical-term recall of up to 95%. For substantially longer guidelines, draft-first extraction achieves the highest recall with selected frontier models, reaching up to 97%. Safety-oriented approaches improve precision but introduce systematic omissions, and multi-stage filtering further amplifies this trade-off. Conclusions: Line-number selection provides a robust alternative to rewriting-based RAG for accessing organisational documentation. Drafting-based approaches may offer additional benefits in very long-document settings. These findings highlight the importance of adapting retrieval strategies to document structure, model scale and the risks of omission.

documents.abstract: BackgroundExcavation work carries some of the most severe fatal-injury risks in construction, yet serious events reflect gaps between formal provisions and field practice. Managers' and workers' perceptions of excavation safety remain underexamined in Türkiye.ObjectiveTo examine how managers and workers evaluate the importance and adequacy of occupational health and safety (OHS) practices, the applications they report relative to the hierarchy of controls, the problems they identify, and the solutions they propose.MethodsA qualitative descriptive field study was conducted with 52 participants (20 managers, 32 workers) on excavation projects in an industrial province of Türkiye. A three-member team conducted interviews in Turkish, supported by observation, field notes, and a reflexive diary. The corpus was analysed through iterative coding and constant comparison, with each participant assigned to one mutually exclusive principal-response category per question and counts reported by role.ResultsAlmost all participants regarded OHS as important (96%), yet most judged implementation inadequate (58%), with workers more critical (63%) than managers (50%). Reported controls concentrated in sloping and benching (27%) and combined administrative measures and PPE (15%); shoring (8%) and shielding (4%) were marginal. Absence of safety culture was the most frequently identified problem (23%) and the most frequently proposed solution (17%). Managers more often emphasised compliance and awareness deficits, workers cave-ins and soil-analysis errors.ConclusionsThe findings indicate a gap between the high stated importance of OHS and its perceived implementation. More consistent use of context-appropriate engineering controls, dynamic risk assessment, and structured worker participation may help reduce this gap.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Safety of enteral nutrition (EN) and parenteral nutrition (PN) products depends on manufacturing quality and changes during storage, preparation, and administration. This critical narrative review examines microbiological, chemical, and physicochemical hazards, distinguishing finished-product measurements, experimental models, and patient outcomes. The evidence documents secondary microbial contamination, material-derived plasticizer exposure, and oxidative changes in selected formulations, while also identifying conditions in which administration introduces no measurable additional contamination. Mechanistic susceptibility of eicosapentaenoic acid and docosahexaenoic acid to oxidation does not establish harmful exposure from contemporary commercial products. We propose Patient-Exposure-Oriented Nutritional Product Safety (PEONPS), a framework linking release quality, post-release change, terminal-line quality, and delivered exposure. Its proposed contribution is to integrate hazard-specific measurements with time-resolved administered dose and a prespecified test of whether the additional information changes a safety decision. Existing exposure studies provide precedents; PEONPS does not claim to introduce exposure assessment itself. Validation should compare its incremental value with established manufacturing, compounding, and administration controls. The framework offers a testable research agenda for targeted safety assessment, rather than a validated clinical score or a requirement for routine bedside testing. Supplementary targeted checks of official standards and selected safety-event and workflow studies were used to contextualize mechanical integrity and human factors; these searches were not intended to constitute exhaustive systematic retrieval.

Objectives Recent outbreaks of accelerated silicosis among engineered stone workers have shown that industrial processing can generate intense exposure to crystalline silica. Diatomaceous earth is widely used in cosmetic modelling facial masks and is generally regarded as low risk; however, calcination can convert its silica structure into cristobalite, a highly toxic crystalline form. We investigated silicosis in workers manufacturing cosmetic modelling facial masks using calcined diatomaceous earth. Methods Following identification of a sentinel case through occupational disease surveillance, we investigated workers employed in cosmetic modelling facial mask manufacturing. All workers had been exposed to calcined diatomaceous earth. Clinical evaluation included pulmonary function testing, chest radiography classified using international criteria and CT. Personal air sampling and bulk material analyses were conducted to characterise crystalline silica exposure. Results Among 18 workers who underwent the temporary occupational health examination, two met International Labour Organization (ILO) chest radiograph criteria for silicosis and five additional workers had low-dose chest CT (LDCT) findings consistent with silicosis despite chest radiographs not meeting the ILO profusion threshold. With the sentinel case, eight workers were identified as silicosis cases. All three chest radiograph-confirmed cases had large opacity category A on chest radiography and LDCT findings consistent with progressive massive fibrosis. Respiratory symptoms were uncommon, and pulmonary function was largely preserved. Measured cristobalite concentrations exceeded the Korean occupational exposure limit, and bulk material analysis revealed high cristobalite content. Conclusions Silicosis can occur in cosmetic manufacturing settings traditionally considered low risk and may be under-recognised when relying on chest radiography alone. Calcination of diatomaceous earth can generate hazardous crystalline silica exposures not captured by conventional industry-based classifications, supporting the need for exposure-based hazard reassessment and enhanced surveillance.
topics: Interstitial Lung Diseases and Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis

documents.abstract: Objective Shift work is an inherent characteristic of the nursing profession. Its detrimental effects extend beyond the physiological level, yet the resulting sleep-related worry is often overlooked. This study aimed to assess the level of sleep-related worry among shift-work nurses and identify factors independently associated with it. Methods A cross-sectional survey using convenience sampling was conducted among 326 shift-work nurses from January to March 2026. Data were collected using a General Information Questionnaire, the Anxiety and Preoccupation about Sleep Questionnaire, Athens Insomnia Scale, Social Support Rating Scale, General Self-Efficacy Scale, and Copenhagen Burnout Inventory. Multiple linear regression was employed to determine factors independently associated with sleep-related worry. Results The total score for sleep-related worry was 35 (28, 41). Spearman correlation analysis indicated that sleep-related worry was positively correlated with insomnia severity ( r = 0.638, p < 0.001) and occupational burnout ( r = 0.519, p < 0.001), and negatively correlated with social support ( r = −0.254, p < 0.001) and general self-efficacy ( r = −0.309, p < 0.001). Multiple linear regression analysis revealed that insomnia severity ( β = 0.449, p < 0.001), occupational burnout ( β = 0.154, p = 0.007), general self-efficacy ( β = −0.110, p = 0.013), and use of sleep medication in the past 6 months ( β = 0.151, p < 0.001) were independently associated with sleep-related worry. However, social support was not independently associated with sleep-related worry in the multiple linear regression model. Conclusion Sleep-related worry among shift-work nurses is at a relatively high level. Interventions addressing self-efficacy, burnout, and sleep health should be incorporated into institutional occupational health policies, alongside legislative measures to protect nurses’ psychological health and ensure adequate rest and recovery.

Students are adopting LLMs at scale. This poses a question: does unrestricted AI access bypass the cognitive effort required for learning, or does it streamline knowledge acquisition? This paper reports on a study where we compare three designs for user-AI interaction in a learning context: (1) an unrestricted conversational bot like ChatGPT, (2) a pedagogically constrained bot that guides through hints without giving final answers, which we refer to as the Socratic mode; and (3) a non-conversational adaptive tutoring system that adjusts difficulty in real-time based on the user’s cognitive engagement derived from the brain signals. Fifty study participants were tasked with learning about nuclear safety protocols, a domain chosen for its zero-prior knowledge baseline. The participants progressed through an instructional video, a pre-test, an AI-driven assessment phase, which varied in the three conditions, and an immediate post-test. The nature of the questions centered primarily on factual knowledge acquisition, but it still required participants to have a global understanding of the concepts in order to answer the questions correctly. A Muse headband was used to derive the cognitive engagement of all users in all conditions. The unrestricted chatbot produced higher learning gains (delta) than both constrained modes ( p <.03, d > 0.80), while the adaptive condition generated significantly higher EEG engagement ( p =.018). The cluster analysis of chatbot usage and discussion patterns by users showed that most participants in the unrestricted-mode adopted a direct answer-retrieval strategy, while participants in the Socratic-mode initially attempted to reason through the hints before progressively disengaging. Consequently, this also suggests that the success of the unrestricted AI is not an evidence of deeper learning, but rather a result of the immediate post-test evaluation after the training phase.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: This article examines how ecological citizenship is differentially enacted by residents in Singapore through everyday waste practices. It argues that household waste management is a key site through which the state governs environmental conduct by framing waste routines as civic responsibility and mobilising residents to sustain a highly engineered sociotechnical regime. Drawing on a stratified household survey of 672 respondents conducted between December 2024 and January 2025, complemented by interviews with residents, the study develops an Ecological Citizenship Index (ECI) based on waste-related behaviours, perceived responsibility and environmental awareness. It shows that ecological citizenship is shaped less by ethnicity or income than by unequal capacities linked to education, gendered domestic labour, work constraints, housing conditions and neighbourhood infrastructure. The Singaporean eco-citizen thus emerges as a socially differentiated subject. More broadly, the article contributes to debates on environmental governmentality and post-political environmentalism by highlighting how responsibilisation sustains urban order.

Abstract Visual Foundation Models (VFMs), such as DINO and CLIP, excel in semantic understanding of images but exhibit limited spatial reasoning capabilities, which limits their applicability to embodied systems. As a result, recent work has incorporated some 3D tasks (such as depth estimation) into VFM training. However, VFM performance remains inconsistent across other spatial tasks, raising the question of whether these models truly possess spatial awareness or overfit to specific 3D objectives. To address this question, we introduce the Spatial Relation Recognition Task (SpaRRTa) benchmark, which evaluates the ability of VFMs to identify static directional relations between visible objects. Unlike traditional 3D objectives that focus on precise metric prediction (e.g., surface normal estimation), SpaRRTa probes a fundamental capability underpinning more advanced forms of human-like spatial understanding. SpaRRTa generates an arbitrary number of photorealistic images with diverse scenes and fully controllable object arrangements, along with freely accessible spatial annotations. Evaluating a range of state-of-the-art VFMs, we reveal significant disparities in their ability to encode directional spatial relations. Through our analysis, we provide insights into the mechanisms that support or hinder this form of spatial awareness in modern VFMs. We hope that SpaRRTa will serve as a useful tool for guiding the development of future spatially aware visual models. Our project page can be found at https://sparrta.gmum.net/ .
topics: Advanced Image and Video Retrieval Techniques

documents.abstract: Despite the steady growth of fast-charging networks under government subsidies, the impact of spatial and ownership structures of charging points on pricing strategies of charging point operators (CPOs) and consumer welfare is poorly understood. Given EVs’ limited range, the competition in a fast-charging network is inherently regional. It is unclear whether and under what circumstances CPOs’ competition can lead to regional monopoly, which may hinder the transition to electric mobility. In this paper, we develop a novel framework to examine the competitive dynamics in fast-charging networks that serve regional demand, incorporating delay costs arising from congestion and locational attractiveness of charging stations. At the core of our framework is a spatial competition model, which characterizes the strategic interactions between CPOs and consumers. To overcome tractability issues associated with large networks that arise from real-world settings, we propose a computationally efficient method to optimize CPOs’ pricing decisions. We instantiate the framework in Germany’s Deutschlandnetz, whose awarded regional network comprises 900 charging stations. Using demand projections for 2030, we conduct a series of counterfactual simulations. Our analysis generates four sets of findings. First, price exhibits a strong negative correlation with the local competitiveness level (measured by the density of charging stations), but shows no clear dependence on absolute demand levels. Second, CPOs’ profits are shaped by both local competitiveness and absolute demand. Third, a uniform, stringent price cap may create inefficiencies in network utilization and discourage infrastructure investment, particularly in less lucrative regions. Finally, spatial and ownership constraints in tender rules may fail to ensure competitive outcomes in large-scale charging networks, allowing CPOs to strategically select locations that strengthen their market power ex post. Taken together, these findings suggest that policymakers should enable regionally equitable access to fast charging while ensuring efficient network utilization.

Learning separate routes does not necessarily establish how they connect or how places on different routes are positioned relative to one another. This study examined how across-route integration varied with route structural complexity and navigation support in immersive VR. Forty students learned two routes separately, then followed a connecting route. Basic guidance was compared with an enhanced interface providing turn previews, distance, and landmark cues. Spatial knowledge was assessed through within- and across-route judgments and cognitive-map reconstruction. In the primary analyses, across-route direction and distance errors were larger in the complex layout, whereas within-route differences were smaller. Cognitive maps showed fewer successful reconstructions of route connections (40.0% vs. 72.5% in the simple layout) and lower similarity to constituent route shapes and landmark configurations. Enhanced guidance produced no reliable improvement in these outcomes. These findings associate the complex layout with poorer knowledge of both route configurations and their connections.

Purpose This study aims to investigate the strategic futures of business-to-business (B2B) marketing by identifying the interlinked themes shaping its transformation, with particular attention to artificial intelligence (AI) as a cross-cutting force embedded in sociotechnical and institutional developments. Design/methodology/approach A two-round Delphi study with 29C-level industry experts was conducted. Responses were coded into 192 thematic mentions across 16 themes, analyzed through co-occurrence mapping and classified in a dual-axis typology by perceived nature (opportunity vs challenge) and origin (sociotechnical vs institutional). Findings AI is central but rarely operates in isolation: it co-occurs with every other theme, functioning as the connective node between internal capabilities and external demands in interorganizational relationships. The typology reveals a statistically significant attribution asymmetry (χ2(1) = 40.23, p < 0.001): internally buildable themes are framed as opportunities, externally imposed demands as challenges. Originality/value The paper theorizes AI not as a tool within the firm but as a boundary-spanning coordination mechanism coupling sociotechnical and institutional domains. The dual-axis typology, tested attribution asymmetry and three propositions provide a foresight-driven framework for understanding strategic readiness in B2B transformation.

This study explored how seventh-grade students demonstrated situational interest during English reading comprehension and described how their language backgrounds appeared in their learning experiences and responses at SMP Cinta Rakyat 3 Pematangsiantar. A descriptive qualitative design involved 30 students from Class VII-F. Data were collected through classroom observations, semi-structured interviews with 10 purposively selected students, and open-ended questionnaires completed by 30 students. The data were analyzed through data condensation, data display, and conclusion drawing and verification. The findings showed that situational interest appeared through emotional response, interest-related cognitive engagement, and perceived value. Students described enjoyment and comfort during guided or shared reading, but some also experienced nervousness, fear, and hesitation during individual reading. Cognitive engagement appeared through asking questions, seeking clarification, repeating unfamiliar words, listening to pronunciation, and recalling previously encountered vocabulary. Students perceived English as useful for communication, vocabulary development, education, future employment, and understanding digital content. Their language backgrounds included Indonesian, Simalungun, Batak, Batak Toba, Malay, and Karo. Daily language use varied according to communication contexts, while previous English exposure came from formal learning, digital media, games, songs, books, films, and social interaction. The study presents language backgrounds as contextual information and does not establish a causal relationship between language background and situational interest.

Abstract Background Community health workers (CHWs) are essential to healthcare delivery in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) yet face increasing threats from extreme heat events (EHEs) due to climate change. Occupational health policies for CHWs remain fragmented globally, with CHWs receiving less attention than workers in other industries despite their critical frontline role. This scoping review aimed to identify barriers and facilitators affecting CHWs during EHEs and determine implementation strategies to support heat safety. Methods We conducted a scoping review by performing a systematic search across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and grey literature published between 2000 and 2024, yielding 1,386 records. After screening, 20 studies met the inclusion criteria. Data synthesis applied the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) to categorize barriers and facilitators, while the CFIR-ERIC matching tool mapped these to implementation strategies from the Expert Recommendations for Implementing Change (ERIC) taxonomy. Results CHWs in LMICs are central to climate-health responses, and also uniquely vulnerable to heat exposure. Widespread barriers to safe and effective service delivery during EHEs include physical challenges (such as dehydration, heat stress, and exhaustion), psychological stress linked to community expectations, inadequate infrastructure (notably poor cooling and inconsistent utilities), chronic underfunding restricting salaries and supplies, insufficient climate-health training, limited policymaker awareness of heat-health issues, and poor community health-seeking behaviors. Key facilitators that support CHWs include their strong community commitment and trust, deep contextual knowledge, disaster preparedness capabilities, and growing grassroots engagement in heat resilience efforts. However, CHWs remain frequently excluded from intervention design and strategic decision-making. The review identified 43 ERIC implementation strategies tailored to address the unique challenges and opportunities for supporting CHWs during EHEs. Of these, 65% served dual functions: mitigating barriers and reinforcing facilitators. Top-priority cross-cutting strategies included resource-sharing agreements, continuous training, promoting system adaptability, offering clinical supervision, creating educational materials, and coalition-building among stakeholders. Conclusions Many implementation strategies exist to both facilitate CHWs’ responding during EHEs and to protect them during those events. However, success depends on contextual adaptation, with interventions addressing local heat-health risks and socio-political contexts. These findings underline the need to take action to support CHWs during EHEs.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: The rapid expansion of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) marks a turning point in language education, accelerating the shift from traditional methodologies toward AI-enhanced learning environments. The aim of this article is to examine the impact of GenAI on language education, understood not as a complementary tool but as a linguistic and epistemological disruption that transforms processes of language production, evaluation, and acquisition. Drawing on a documentary analysis that integrates recent theoretical, empirical, and regulatory sources, the study addresses four interrelated objectives: to reorganize instructional design toward generative tasks of greater cognitive complexity; to identify pedagogical applications of GenAI through tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, NotebookLM, ElevenLabs, Canva, HeyGen, and other emerging GenAI systems; to redefine the teacher’s role as a critical orchestrator and AI-literate professional; and to examine the ethical and linguistic challenges posed by GenAI, including hallucination, discourse homogenization, and risks to academic integrity. The findings indicate that GenAI enhances learning only when embedded within intentional, critically mediated, and well-supervised pedagogy that preserves cognitive engagement, linguistic diversity, and educational equity.[La rápida expansión de la inteligencia artificial generativa (IAGen) marca un punto de inflexión en la enseñanza de lenguas, impulsando la transición desde métodos tradicionales hacia entornos de aprendizaje enriquecidos por IA. El objetivo de este artículo es examinar el impacto de la IAGen en la enseñanza de lenguas, entendida no como una herramienta complementaria, sino como una disrupción lingüística y epistemológica que transforma los procesos de producción, evaluación y adquisición del lenguaje. Mediante un análisis documental que integra fuentes teóricas, empíricas y normativas recientes, el estudio persigue cuatro objetivos específicos: reorganizar el diseño didáctico hacia actividades generativas de mayor complejidad cognitiva; identificar formas de implementación de la IAGen a través de herramientas como ChatGPT, Claude, NotebookLM, ElevenLabs, Canva o HeyGen; redefinir el rol docente como orquestador crítico y profesional con alfabetización en IA; y examinar los desafíos éticos y lingüísticos derivados de la IAGen, como la alucinación, la homogeneización del discurso o los riesgos para la integridad académica. Los resultados del análisis indican que la IAGen solo mejora el aprendizaje cuando se integra en una pedagogía intencional, crítica y supervisada que preserve el compromiso cognitivo, la diversidad lingüística y la equidad educativa].
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The convergence of artificial intelligence, big data, and other engineering technologies with clinical medicine has catalyzed the emergence of the interdisciplinary discipline of Intelligent Medical Engineering, which demands the cultivation of compound professionals integrating medical literacy, engineering competencies, and innovative thinking. As the core foundational course underpinning this discipline, Introduction to Basic Medicine remains a newly established offering lacking mature pedagogical paradigms and aligned experimental teaching systems. Conventional pure medical basic instruction models are misaligned with the cognitive attributes and training objectives of students with engineering backgrounds. This study developed and operationalized a full-cycle pedagogical reform framework oriented toward medical-engineering interdisciplinary integration to systematically construct students’ medical knowledge architecture, foster interdisciplinary thinking, and enhance capacities for independent learning, practical application, and innovation. This study employed action research coupled with quasi-experimental pedagogical practice. This pedagogical reform endeavor was predicated on two core innovative dimensions: the systematic integrated restructuring of interdisciplinary curricular content, and the construction of a closed-loop instructional paradigm encompassing pre-class preparatory activities, in-class interactive instruction, and post-class tiered consolidation. A diversified assessment framework integrating formative evaluation and summative examination was developed. A comprehensive set of evaluation metrics, including student academic performance, reliability analysis of survey instruments, classroom engagement metrics, and post-course interview feedback, was employed to appraise teaching effectiveness. The cross-institutional integrated pedagogical reform was associated with favorable shifts in student learning outcomes. It correlated with augmented autonomous learning efficiency, consolidated mastery of basic medical knowledge, and improved interdisciplinary cognitive competence. The empirical investigation further delineated prevailing limitations, encompassing inadequate depth of interdisciplinary practical components, suboptimal execution of differentiated tiered instruction, and ambiguous formative assessment criteria, alongside targeted optimization strategies. The medical-engineering integrated full-cycle instructional framework presents a transferable, empirically validated paradigm for foundational medical education in interdisciplinary majors implemented via cross-institutional collaborative training, and delivers a methodological reference for curriculum development and pedagogical innovation in emerging medical-engineering disciplines.

Background Postoperative complications after adult noncardiac surgery are frequent and strongly associated with mortality, prolonged morbidity, functional decline, and organizational burden. Because not all complications are preventable, failure to rescue has emerged as a central concept reflecting the capacity of healthcare organizations to recognize and treat deterioration in time. Methods We conducted a critical narrative review using SANRA as a quality self-appraisal framework. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched for publications from 2000 to 2026, complemented by backward and forward citation tracking. The review focused on adult, non-obstetric patients recovering after noncardiac surgery, primarily in general surgical wards. Results Perioperative risk models, early warning scores, electronic health record-integrated and artificial intelligence-enabled systems, and continuous monitoring devices have improved the acquisition and integration of physiological and clinical information. However, prediction and detection do not themselves establish clinical effectiveness. These technologies primarily strengthen signal acquisition, recognition, and alert generation, whereas patient benefit depends on timely reassessment, diagnostic interpretation, escalation, treatment, and available response resources. Implementation studies improve process outcomes more consistently than patient-important outcomes. Benefit is most apparent when surveillance is linked to an explicit, procedure-specific diagnostic and therapeutic pathway. Human and organizational factors influence every stage of this process. Discussion Postoperative rescue is a sociotechnical process rather than a purely technological intervention. Current evidence supports linking deterioration alerts to explicit and adequately resourced response pathways, but effects on mortality, serious complications, disability, and recovery remain uncertain. Future studies should combine component-level and integrated-system evaluation while incorporating patient-important, process, and staff outcomes.

Background: Nurses experience occupational and personal stress, which can reduce well-being and life satisfaction and contribute to burnout. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effect of progressive relaxation exercises (PRE) on nurses’ life satisfaction, comfort, and burnout. Methods: This randomized controlled trial included nurses from a tertiary care hospital. The intervention consisted of PRE involving the sequential contraction and relaxation of major muscle groups. The intervention group performed PRE for 5 weeks, three times a week, with each session lasting 20 minutes, outside active working hours. Outcomes were assessed using the Satisfaction with Life Scale, Nurse Comfort Questionnaire, and Maslach Burnout Inventory. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, chi-square, t-tests, and repeated-measures ANOVA in SPSS 25.0. Results: After five weeks, the intervention group showed significantly higher life satisfaction (18.06±2.97 vs. 12.50±2.52, p < 0.001), total comfort (115.63±14.64 vs. 100.73±13.49, p < 0.001), and personal accomplishment (30.26±3.35 vs. 27.30±5.01, p = 0.009) scores than the control group. In contrast, emotional exhaustion (25.76±5.59 vs. 29.63±5.82, p = 0.011) and depersonalization (11.23±3.51 vs. 15.13±3.13, p < 0.001) were significantly lower in the intervention group. Conclusions/Application to Practice: PRE reduced nurses’ burnout and enhanced their life satisfaction and comfort. It can be recommended as a simple and reliable complementary method to support nurses’ well-being. Occupational health professionals can integrate brief, structured PRE sessions into workplace wellness programs, enabling nurses to perform standardized exercises independently during breaks or outside working hours. This practical approach may support nurses’ psychological well-being without disrupting patient care or workflow.

Leaders often strive to foster psychological safety in teams, and yet it may not emerge. This study builds grounded theory on how psychological safety emerges, or not, on teams. We draw on longitudinal ethnographic data from a matched pair case study of two teams over two years, including verbatim meeting transcripts that elicit the micro-processes affecting psychological safety and interviews that elucidate team members’ interpretations. We identify an illusion initially present on both teams in which surface markers of psychological safety existed but team members nonetheless continued to avoid interpersonal risk—what we call a psychological safety mirage. This occurred because external pressures on leaders spurred them to take self-protective actions that inadvertently reinforced interpersonal risk, despite their continued efforts to invite contributions. One team was eventually able to break from this mirage through a three-phase de-risking process that facilitated psychological safety emergence: (1) collectively recognizing the underlying risk faced by team members, (2) de-risking contributions by offering opportunities to build skills, through which safety was demonstrated and reinforced, and (3) enacting psychological safety, with all team members contributing, reinforcing, and sharing in the benefits of reduced interpersonal risk. This paper advances theory on psychological safety by conceptualizing a team-level de-risking process model that facilitates its emergence and by characterizing its mirage.

Psychosocial hazards can compromise more than worker wellbeing. In safety–critical systems, sustained workload and uncertainty can combine with reduced recovery to weaken the human and organisational capacities through which risks are recognised and controlled. This study develops a systems model of how psychosocial demands, leadership buffering, and boundary disruption can constrain sustained adaptation while operations continue. We examine these dynamics among middle-level leaders in Australia’s mining, oil, and gas sector during the prolonged COVID-19 crisis. Positioned between executive decision-making and frontline operations, these leaders translated changing directives into operating practice while carrying responsibility for continuity and employee wellbeing. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 24 managers and eight general managers. Team-based thematic analysis was supported by a cross-case descriptive matrix of recurring conditions. Leaders described isolation and disconnection alongside work intensification and fatigue. Persistent uncertainty was often accompanied by anxiety. As organisational arrangements changed, leadership roles expanded and work–nonwork boundaries became more permeable. Middle-level leaders buffered competing organisational and workforce demands, helping operations continue while opportunities for recovery narrowed. Participants described growing difficulty sustaining adaptive effort. The model distinguishes adaptive performance from adaptive sustainability. Continued functioning may coexist with depletion of the resources that enable further adaptation. We extend safety science by conceptualising psychosocial risk as a dynamic organisational process and identifying middle-level leaders as potential sources of safety intelligence. Effective control requires organisations to address how work itself generates exposure, including the staffing and authority available to leaders. Boundary protection and recovery should sit alongside individual support.

This study examines the influence of Sustainable Social Supply Chain Practices (SSSCPs) on Supplier Performance (SP) in the manufacturing industry of Sleman Regency, Indonesia. Primary data were collected through questionnaires and analyzed using linear regression to investigate the relationship between the variables. The empirical findings indicate that SSSCPs positively influence supplier performance. The study focuses on medium-sized and large manufacturing companies that have operated for at least 10 years in Sleman Regency. The findings emphasize the importance of maintaining ethical labor standards, providing regular training programs for local communities, complying with occupational health and safety regulations throughout the supply chain, and preventing child labor and forced labor. Theoretically, this study contributes to the existing literature by providing empirical evidence of the relationship between social sustainability practices and supplier performance in a developing-country context. Practically, the findings offer valuable insights for manufacturing companies seeking to enhance supplier performance, strengthen supply chain sustainability, and improve overall organizational competitiveness through the implementation of socially responsible supply chain practices.
topics: Global trade, sustainability, and social impact

documents.abstract: The KIP (Knowledge Is Power) dataset compiles and transforms the visual content from 165 issues of the Chinese magazine Zhishi Jiushi Liliang [Knowledge Is Power] and the Soviet magazine of the same title, Знание – сила [Knowledge Is Power], from 1956 to 1962. The captioned images are cropped from scans of the physical copies of the cover artworks (color), drawings (black-and-white), photographs (color and black-and-white), and artistic title lettering. The dataset contains 13,896 images (in PNG format) for historians of sciences and technology to study the shared sociotechnical imageries excavated from a transitional period in the Soviet bloc, where current archives on the same period are focused almost exclusively on textual data. The project is intended for researchers and scholars, and the KIP dataset is in no way a market substitute for the original magazines or their high-resolution digital copies.

Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly deployed in organizations, yet employees differ substantially and persistently in how frequently and intensively they use it. This workplace “usage divide” raises a fundamental but underexplored question: Why do employees differ systematically in their use of GenAI, even under common formal access? We argue that this divide reflects a broader challenge for IS research: explaining the use of systems that are probabilistic rather than deterministic, and general-purpose yet uneven and evolving in their capabilities. In workplaces where employees remain accountable for task performance, these properties make the use of GenAI not a routine adoption decision but a judgment process in which employees assess the system’s credibility and determine where task-relevant expertise lies. Drawing on molecular genetics and metacognition research, we theorize that genetic propensity, indexed by the educational attainment polygenic score (PGS)—an aggregate genetic index associated with educational attainment—helps account for systematic variation in these judgments and, ultimately, persistent differences in workplace GenAI use. Specifically, we develop a parsimonious two-pathway model linking educational attainment PGS to GenAI use: a cognitive pathway involving formal educational attainment and perceptions of GenAI credibility, and a metacognitive pathway involving strategic mindset and metaknowledge of where task-relevant expertise lies. We test our model using a multisource dataset combining primary genetic data, survey measures, and 21 months of objective usage logs. The results show that educational attainment PGS, a broad distal genetic index, is associated with both GenAI use frequency and interaction intensity and provide theory-consistent evidence for the proposed pathways. Overall, our study offers a micro-foundational account of the persistent GenAI usage divide and advances IS theory on the use of probabilistic, general-purpose systems in the workplace.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is being investigated across the gastric cancer care pathway, but the evidence required for clinical adoption extends beyond predictive accuracy. This narrative review critically exam ines AI applications in endoscopy, computed tomography, digital pathology, multimodal modeling, tumor microenvironment assessment, molecular profiling, and surgical assistance. Selected studies demonstrate substantial progress in lesion detection, staging, response prediction, and prognostic stratification. However, retrospective discrimination, prospective validation, and improved outcomes under AI-guided care represent distinct evidentiary achievements. A large randomized endoscopy trial illustrates this distinction: AI reduced examination blind spots but did not significantly improve the primary endpoint of gastric neoplasm detection after pathology review. Elsewhere, externally validated imaging and pathology models remain vulnerable to differences in acquisition protocols, patient selection, treatment context, and data availability. Associations between model scores and treatment outcomes cannot establish that a score identifies differential treatment benefit. Multimodal and molecular approaches introduce additional challenges related to missing inputs, as say reproducibility, and implementation costs. We propose a staged translational framework linking a clearly defined clinical decision to independent validation, prospective workflow evaluation, comparative impact assessment, and monitored deployment. Priorities include clinically appropriate reference standards, calibration and threshold-specific performance, subgroup evaluation, transparent reporting, human factors testing, and economic assessment. Clinical adoption should depend on reproducible incremental value within a specified care pathway, with safeguards proportionate to the consequences of error. These requirements provide a practical basis for converting promising gastric cancer AI models into reliable clinical tools. Keywords: gastric cancer; artificial intelligence; clinical translation; multimodal learning; precision oncology; clinical utility
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Unsignalized roundabouts remain challenging for connected and autonomous vehicles because of dynamic merges, spatial conflicts, and communication constraints. We present a decentralized coordination architecture based on Group Mutual Exclusion (GME), in which each conflict point is treated as a local critical section and compatible virtual platoons may be admitted concurrently. A lead vehicle aggregates requests from its physical queue and relays admission decisions to following vehicles. To make this safety-critical process intelligible to occupants, we introduce a query-driven small language model (SLM) interface that reads structured controller traces and produces explanations only when requested. The SLM is strictly read-only and cannot alter GME decisions. We illustrate how traces containing conflict, priority, and waiting-time information can support contextual explanations of yielding, deceleration, and merging. The work provides an architecture and feasibility demonstration. Quantitative traffic, language-model, and human-factors evaluations are left to future work.

Abstract Background Cancer treatment can be associated with numerous direct and indirect financial burdens. These burdens, described as financial toxicity, can often affect care-based decision making of cancer patients. Breast cancer is the leading cause of cancer death of women in India, who often face the detrimental effects of financial toxicity. Measuring financial toxicity can be assessed through the COST-FACIT-V2 questionnaire, yet it is only available in limited languages. This study aimed to translate the widely used COST-FACIT-V2 tool, to be used for assessing financial toxicity in Odia, one of India’s most commonly spoken regional languages. Methods We followed the tool-developer guidelines for translating, validating and culturally adapting the COST-FACIT-V2 tool for use in an Odia-speaking population in India. This entailed a forward translation and back translation, facilitated by artificial intelligence (AI), confirmed by human review, and pilot testing with four native Odia speaking breast cancer patients and six native Odia speaking healthcare workers at a comprehensive cancer center in Odisha, India. Results The AI forward and back translations demonstrated accuracy with human review. Minor changes were needed to enhance contextual accuracy and consistency. The key concept “paid work at home” was not well understood by the pilot sample group, leading to culturally adapted modifications in the final translated version. Discussion The findings of this paper support the linguistic accuracy and cultural appropriateness of the Odia COST-FACIT-V2 and highlight the importance of rigorous translation methods to enable equitable measurement of financial toxicity and inform financial protection efforts in diverse cancer care settings. The use of AI represents a potentially complementary tool for supporting translation of standardized instruments used in health systems research.
topics: Economic and Financial Impacts of Cancer

documents.abstract: Healthcare schools must assign students to a limited number of internship places, and the process must satisfy department rotation, internship round, institution uniqueness, ward capacity, and preference rules. Manual planning is slow and automated results can also be difficult to inspect and explain. This study compares a capacity-constrained regret heuristic with mixed-integer linear programming (MILP). The heuristic uses the feasible options available at each decision, while the MILP reduces total weighted cost across the cohort. Method-specific evidence records support a separate explanation step with the Gemini 3 Model. The scheduling experiments used 133 students and produced 399 valid placements with each method. The baseline MILP cost was 5275.2, which was 3.5% below the heuristic cost of 5467.5. The median runtimes were 124.98 s for MILP and 1.10 s for the heuristic. The heuristic completed the 75% and 50% capacity cases. The corresponding MILP cases reached the ten-minute limit without a result. Regret reduced the mean heuristic cost by 1.05% against the tested no-regret variants. MILP reduced the mean and median student costs, but both methods had the same maximum student cost of 194.6. The explainability experiment used three cases, two methods, and three experts. All 18 correctness checks were positive. The heuristic received a higher mean score for alternative explanation and depth. Uncertainty scores were equal, and quality scores were similar. The results show a trade-off between cohort cost, runtime, capacity pressure, local decision evidence, and explanation detail.

Appropriate reliance on autonomy in multi-agent systems requires operators to continuously evaluate and assign leadership among heterogeneous autonomous agents as task demands and environmental conditions evolve. Research on human-autonomy collaboration has demonstrated promise for anticipated situations and dyadic interactions, but lacks investigation into how operators calibrate trust and competence assessments to support dynamic leadership assignment across multiple agents during unanticipated events. This study investigates temporal modeling of human leadership assignment to multiple autonomous agents based on real-time trust and competence assessment in multi-agent systems. Thirty-nine participants completed three simulated search-and-rescue scenarios involving four autonomous uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs). Each scenario was comprised of twenty object identification trials. Participants rated trust and ranked competence for each UAV in every trial. Results revealed that participants assigned leadership to UAVs based on both competence and trust assessments with respect to the task and environmental conditions. Participants’ assignment performance improved across successive scenarios as they gained experience with UAV capabilities. Network representations of trust, competence and leadership assignment, termed Trust-Competence-Identity-Networks (TCIN), were constructed for every trial and modeled sequentially using Temporal Exponential Random Graph Models (TERGM) to examine the temporal evolution of human perception and leadership assignment (i.e., UAV reliance). TERGM results indicated that trust reflects personalized assessments developed through interaction experience, while competence represents task-specific assessments for leadership assignment. This research extends reliance research on dyadic interactions to multi-agent interactions, introduces the TCIN for studying leadership or reliance dynamics, and provides practical insights for designing adaptive multi-agent systems.

AI model explanations are intended to support users in forming and updating beliefs regarding model predictions. However, how these explanations shape cognitive belief processes remains under-explored, particularly for complex relational models like Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). We investigate how visually interactive GNN explanations influence belief dynamics through a qualitative, process-tracing think-aloud study (N=20) with domain and AI experts, complemented by descriptive summaries of coded belief processes. Participants interacted with a GNN-based healthcare satisfaction prediction model within an immersive 3D virtual reality (VR) environment. Drawing on a theoretical framework of belief dynamics, we identified how these interactive explanations shaped belief formation, prediction acceptance, and hypothesis specification. Findings reveal that while domain expertise facilitated belief formation through internal knowledge recall, AI expertise supported independent evidence search through structured reasoning strategies. Our results suggest that GNN explanations should transition from static endpoints to interactive prompts that facilitate iterative belief updating.RESEARCH HIGHLIGHTSThink-aloud study (N=20) of domain and AI experts interpreting GNN explanations in VR.Applies the belief understanding framework to trace evidence evaluation in GNN-based XAI.Contributes a reusable codebook mapping belief processes to observable interaction behaviors.GNN explanations acted as prompts for evidence search and hypothesis generation, not endpoints.Domain experts relied on local knowledge recall; AI experts on reasoning about the model.

Purpose Users within the same organization may enact the same digital information system differently, creating diverse requirements and challenges for implementation. It is essential to view information system implementation as a process shaped by individuals' capacity to act within organizational structures, that is, through their agency. This study explores the manifestation of user agency and its associated structural conditions in information system implementation. Design/methodology/approach We examined users' experiences of information system implementation in two industrial companies' maintenance operations, through an interpretive qualitative study based on semi-structured interviews. Findings The study identifies four types of agency, namely eligible, estranged, skilled and motivated, and shows ways in which structural conditions of work design, social relationships and practices and situated individual resources in information system users' work both enable and hinder user's capacity to act during information system implementation. Practical implications The identified agency types can help managers in tailoring information system implementation support. Acknowledging work design, collaborative practices and situated resources enhances users' capacity to act with the new system. Originality/value This study contributes by introducing a typology of user agency in information system implementation: it provides a fine-grained lens to explain why users facing the same information system enact it differently and extends enactment-oriented information system research on human agency. Showing how agency is conditioned by work design, social relationships and practices and situated individual resources in users' unique work conditions, it addresses agency as part of the social and structural dynamics of information system implementation.

Robot Foundation Models (RFMs) and related robot learning techniques represent a promising approach to developing general-purpose home robots. Given the broad capabilities of RFMs, users will inevitably ask an RFM-based robot to perform tasks that the RFM was not trained or evaluated on. In these cases, it is crucial that users understand the risks associated with attempting novel tasks due to the relatively high cost of failure. Furthermore, an informed user who understands an RFM’s capabilities will know what situations and tasks the robot can handle. In this paper, we study how non-experts interpret performance information from RFM and similar robot learning evaluations. These evaluations typically report task success rate (TSR) as the primary performance metric. While TSR is intuitive to experts, it is necessary to validate whether novices also use this information as intended. Toward this end, we conducted a study in which users saw real evaluation data, including TSR, failure case descriptions, and videos from multiple published robot learning projects. The results highlight that non-experts use TSR in a manner consistent with expert expectations and highly value other information types, such as failure cases that are not often reported in RFM evaluations. Furthermore, we find that users want access to both real data from previous evaluations of the RFM and estimates from the robot about how well it will do on a novel task.

Context: In this chapter, the implementation and governance of User-Centered Design (UCD) are analyzed.At present, organizations are adopting the international principles of the ISO 9241-210 standard and moving away from linear software and hardware development schemes.The standard adopts a constructivist approach that places human needs and capabilities at the center of the sociotechnical cycle of technology.Objective: The purpose of the study is to set out the normative epistemology of ISO 9241-210, to distinguish analytically between user-centered and human-centered design, and to describe what the iterative operational cycle consists of, together with the techniques of empirical measurement and participatory co-design.Method: A theoretical-descriptive documentary review was carried out on the basis of international criteria in ergonomics, psychophysical methods for interface evaluation, and co-creation dynamics for information architectures.Results: The findings indicate that iterating through the operational cycle, together with quantitative techniques such as eye-tracking and the SUS and UMUX scales, prevents both the aesthetic trap and cognitive overload.Nevertheless, challenges persist, such as the management of multidisciplinary teams and the reduction of the complex human being to purely instrumental roles.Conclusions: Through cyclical and participatory iteration, companies obtain an auditable process that lowers the costs of subsequent corrective redesign.It is advisable for collaborative design practices to be institutionalized in order to strengthen usability and the reflective dimension of the brand.

Vibe coding is an AI-assisted software development approach in which developers express intent in natural language and large language models generate code. To our knowledge, no review has synthesized academic and practitioner sources under a common protocol. We conducted a multivocal literature review of publications from January 2022 to 9 September 2026, identified through searches in October 2025 and September 2026. After assessing source quality and credibility, we analyzed 266 sources (76 peer-reviewed, 190 grey) across eight research questions: 146 were direct, 93 adjacent, and 27 background. Presence and outcome findings receive reporting-support and evidence-strength labels, respectively. The second author conducted twelve checks; pre-reconciliation agreement was low in several, but substantial for the final directness rule and moderate for the outcome fields, which were checked in full. Sources describe a generation-evaluation-revision loop, with developer work shifting from writing code toward directing, supervising, and validating. Productivity is reported in 109 of the 159 sources contributing to the outcome question, of which 22 provide assertions only; these counts indicate reporting, not effect size. Most comparable sources report short-term productivity gains and long-term maintainability costs, but both receive Weak evidence-strength labels because some comparable sources report opposing directions. Short-term quality and defects are labeled Weak. Long-term productivity, long-term quality, and short-term reproducibility are labeled Moderate. Prototyping is reported more often than production use, and user-interface work more often than data and machine-learning work, but task-domain evidence is sparse. Future work should evaluate safeguards, session-level dynamics, long-term maintainability, and production use.

Electric vehicles’s expansion raises concerns over brake light activation during regenerative braking. This study investigated how regenerative braking deceleration without brake light activation affects drivers’ driving behaviors and subjective workload. A within-subject driving simulator experiment was conducted with 28 licensed drivers under four regenerative braking deceleration levels (0.7, 0.9, 1.1, and 1.3 m/s2) within the current optional brake light activation range. Significant changes in minimum TTC and standard deviation of TTC first emerged between the 0.7 and 0.9 m/s2 conditions. Reaction Time and Brake Force differed significantly between the 0.7 and 1.1 m/s2 conditions, whereas Brake Count differed only between the 1.3 and the 0.7 and 0.9 m/s2 conditions. Subjective driving workload differed only between the 0.9 and 1.3 m/s2 conditions. These findings suggest that TTC-based safety measures were more sensitive than behavioral and subjective measures, identifying 0.9 m/s2 as an empirical candidate for evaluation of brake light activation criteria.

As generative AI enters creative work, practitioners must decide where AI assistance ends and human authorship begins. Human-agent interaction (HAI) research has examined AI as a tool, collaborator, consultant, and competitor. The longitudinal problem is how these roles are revised as systems become more capable, public, and economically embedded. We report a five-year interview study with 17 Chinese digital painters, based on annual semi-structured interviews from 2021 to 2025. Participants described recurring but non-uniform patterns of protective resistance, pragmatic task delegation, and, for some, reflective agency repartitioning. Early resistance protected observation, originality, signature, and ownership from AI. Later delegation placed AI in bounded tasks such as references, backgrounds, rough sketches, and client-facing drafts. By 2025, some participants built hybrid workflows around human-only zones, while others described fatigue, precarity, or difficulty locating a remaining human role. Peer norms, emotional climates, and production pressures shaped which delegations felt useful, acceptable, or exhausting. Copyright, authorship, and creative labor remained recurring limits on what participants were willing to delegate. We frame these accounts as longitudinal agency partitioning, the situated work of deciding which stages, responsibilities, values, and claims remain human in creative human-agent interaction. We discuss design implications for revisable agency-boundary controls, provenance scaffolds, and community-facing authorship norms.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: We present RPO-PDT, an embodied conversational agent that adapts its conversational role to the current participant. It acts as a Personal Development Tutor (PDT) when supporting students and as a simulated student when faculty rehearse tutoring strategies. Voluntary closed-set participant verification informs a confidence-controlled role manager: stable enrolled-faculty matches activate the Student role, while enrolled students and unmatched participants use the default PDT role and uncertain observations cause no transition. The system combines Furhat interaction, Rasa orchestration, institutional retrieval, safeguarding, and LLM-based generation. User control is preserved through manual role override, consent-based facial enrolment, temporary interaction identifiers, and explicit retention or deletion of enrolled profiles. The demonstration exposes both role-switching behaviour and these privacy controls in interaction.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: BackgroundFamily caregivers are often working adults whose unpaid care responsibilities can disrupt paid work, yet occupational impact is rarely examined beyond employment status or financial burden. Burn caregiving provides a high-demand traumatic-injury context in which prolonged rehabilitation, family reorganization, and support needs may conflict with caregivers' work lives.ObjectiveTo examine the occupational impact of burn caregiving over a 24-month recovery period and characterize two theory-informed patterns of caregiver occupational experience: occupational sacrifice and positive occupational appraisal.MethodsWe analyzed baseline and 24-month occupational follow-up data from 256 family caregivers in a burn survivor-caregiver cohort. Follow-up outcomes captured work participation, job change, caregiving-attributed workforce detachment, perceived career impact, and work-related barriers and facilitators post-baseline. Occupational sacrifice was operationalized as caregiving-attributed workforce detachment or adverse career appraisal among employed caregivers; positive occupational appraisal was defined as favorable perceived career impact. Baseline demographic, survivor-injury, and psychosocial characteristics were examined descriptively and in logistic regression models.ResultsAt 24 months, 71.5% reported ongoing work participation, 20.7% caregiving-attributed workforce detachment, and 7.8% other changes. Among employed caregivers, 32.2% reported job change, of whom 42.4% reported negative career appraisal. Occupational sacrifice was identified in 35.2% and was accompanied by functional, appearance-related, family-caregiving, workplace, rehabilitation-support, and financial barriers. Positive occupational appraisal was reported by 31.3% and was associated with lower baseline distress and higher posttraumatic growth.ConclusionsThese findings extend injury-related occupational health to family caregivers and support a theory-informed framework for studying work-caregiving strain, occupational sacrifice, and positive appraisal prospectively.

This study examined the relationship between work–life balance and employee engagement among commercial bank officers in Yenagoa, Bayelsa State, Nigeria. Specifically, it investigated flexible work time, telecommuting, and leave policy in relation to physical, emotional, and cognitive engagement, while examining the moderating role of organisational culture. A cross-sectional survey design was adopted, using a census approach to cover 114 banking offices across seven commercial banks. Of the 114 questionnaires distributed, 108 valid responses were obtained, representing a response rate of 94.7%. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Spearman’s rank-order correlation, and regression analysis in SPSS version 26. Reported Cronbach’s alpha coefficients ranged from .79 to .88. The findings indicated positive associations between all three work–life balance dimensions and the three dimensions of employee engagement. Leave policy had the strongest reported association with cognitive engagement (𝑟𝑠 = .646,𝑝 < .01). The regression results also indicated a significant interaction between work–life balance and organisational culture (𝛽 = .213,𝑝 = .004). The study concludes that work–life balance practices are positively associated with employee engagement in the study setting. It recommends improved leave administration, flexible scheduling where operationally feasible, role-appropriate telecommuting, and a supportive organisational culture.

Purpose The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in workplaces is rapidly increasing in our society. This means that AI is fundamentally reshaping workplaces, how tasks are performed and how the authors interact with colleagues. This study aims to develop explanatory knowledge about the challenges of AI-augmented workplaces. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative and deductive research approach was applied. Key challenges discovered in the literature review were used as predefined themes to identify and analyse empirical data. Findings The authors have identified five key challenges: AI Strategy, AI Education, Control, Meaningfulness and Integrated Work Processes for Human-AI Collaboration. These challenges were examined in terms of their causes and effects, and an explanatory model (AICH) was developed. Research limitations/implications The study collected data from five companies, which provides some generality beyond this study’s empirical domain. However, it poses challenges in making broader generalisations. Future research could be designed as broader studies to confirm, modify or challenge the findings. Practical implications The findings contribute to workplace learning and provide a basis for identifying risks and potential measures. Social implications The identified challenges regarding AI-assisted workplaces will most likely have broader social ramifications, affecting employees’ overall well-being and company culture. Originality/value The authors do not claim that the challenges per se are new. However, the authors claim that the models consisting of explanatory knowledge visualised as cause-and-effect models are new.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: This study advances research on social evaluations by theorizing how partisan media construct CEO infamy through dramaturgical logics distinct from those underlying CEO celebrity. Moving beyond conceptualizations of infamy as merely negative celebrity, we argue that infamy emerges through simple melodramatic narratives casting CEOs as wrongdoers, whereas celebrity involves more complex dramatized narratives portraying CEOs as saviors. Focusing on CEOs’ liberal sociopolitical activism—a visible, ideologically-charged action that departs from conventional executive roles—we theorize that this behavior generates divergent constructions in partisan media: infamy in conservative outlets and celebrity in liberal outlets. We further argue that activism more readily generates infamy than celebrity because melodramatic narratives are simpler to construct and negative deviance is more readily perceived than positive deviance. We examine two moderators of these relationships. Firm performance differentially shapes these constructions, with poorer performance intensifying conservative-media infamy and stronger performance amplifying liberal-media celebrity. CEO social media engagement, conversely, attenuates both by constraining traditional media’s narrative discretion and reducing activism’s newsworthiness. We develop an LLM-based annotation system capturing CEO-directed sentiment, role attributions, and dramaturgical narratives in media articles.
