documents.abstract: I argue for Black pragmatism’s usefulness to organization studies by intervening in debates about the normative foundations of stakeholder theory. Tracing three braided themes within Black pragmatism (tragicomic hope, critical temper, and democratic faith), I show how they both illuminate neglected aspects of the pragmatist themes of inquiry, abduction, and community that have influenced organization studies and extend those concepts to open new avenues of inquiry. I suggest that Black pragmatism reveals how the libertarian assumptions of stakeholder theory are inconsistent with its pragmatist commitments, and that this weakness even applies to recent attempts to center stakeholder theory upon marginalized stakeholders.

Everyday intelligent products increasingly use adaptive components whose actions are constrained by capability, context, uncertainty, and privacy. We introduce bounded adaptive agency, a design framework for making these constraints understandable and controllable. Study 1 interviewed 28 designers and related specialists, identifying four interdependent boundaries: capability, deployment, agency, and interruption. Study 2 tested a boundary-oriented design canvas in a controlled concept-generation task with 54 participants, examining how it shaped early decisions about scope, uncertainty, autonomy, recovery, and interruption. Study 3 evaluated paired adaptive-product scenarios with 462 valid participants, comparing a bundled boundary-oriented configuration with high autonomy while holding product goals and nominal sensing inputs constant. Across the studies, boundedness was most useful when it clarified capability, authority, timing, and recovery without sacrificing product value. These findings offer a traceable framework for calibrating adaptive behavior in human–AI interaction and intelligent-product design.

This study examines how clarification interaction mode and personalization level jointly influence task efficiency and user experience in e-commerce service encounters. In a 2 × 3 between-subjects experiment, 60 participants were randomly assigned to six conditions and completed five after-sales tasks. Objective performance was assessed by completion time; subjective evaluations included perceived warmth, perceived competence, perceived privacy risk, interaction satisfaction, and cognitive effort. The five completion-time outcomes were analyzed using MANOVA, followed by exploratory task-specific two-way ANOVAs. Selection mode was associated with shorter completion times in each of the five service scenarios and with higher perceived competence and interaction satisfaction than open-input clarification. Exploratory follow-up analyses identified statistically significant personalization effects in some scenarios, and personalization level was associated only with perceived competence among subjective measures. Because task was not modeled as a within-subject factor, these findings do not establish that personalization effects differed statistically across tasks.

Numerical countdown formats may influence comparative judgments of waiting time. We compared six integer-only and decimal countdown formats on participants’ own smartphones. Experiment 1 measured paired judgments of countdown duration, whereas Experiment 2 measured paired judgments of site loading speed in a web-application-like task. One-decimal-place displays tended to receive longer or slower judgments than several alternatives. In the 10-second condition, formats with two to five decimal places received shorter or faster judgments than integer-only and one-decimal-place formats in both experiments, although differences within the two-to-five-decimal group varied between experiments. These results describe relative judgments among the tested formats, not an absolute reduction in perceived waiting time. Because decimal precision and updating behavior were not manipulated independently, the findings concern the formats as implemented rather than digit count alone. They provide conditional guidance for comparing countdown formats in interface design.

Dashboards are central to contemporary organizations aiming to ‘datafy’ decision making and management practices. As one of the primary media through which people engage with digital data in organizational contexts, dashboards shape how data is accessed and perceived. Despite their ubiquity, there is limited understanding of how dashboards mediate data visibility and influence observers’ perceptions of the data. Drawing on theories of mediation and diagrammatics, this paper analyzes the ‘generic form’ shared by all dashboards. It then identifies the modes of observation encouraged by dashboards, revealing how they position their observers. While grounded in theoretical arguments, the analysis incorporates empirical examples from a study on the datafication of Human Resource Management. The paper makes two key contributions. It emphasizes the critical role of visual forms in datafication processes, and it highlights the organizational implications of the use of a specific kind of visual medium: the dashboard.

Shared e-scooters are now common in urban transportation, but safety planning remains limited by a lack of exposure-based, spatially detailed crash risk measures. This study applied an exposure-based approach to identify high-risk e-scooter corridors in Nashville, Tennessee, combining 92 police-reported, motor-vehicle-involved e-scooter crashes with trip-kilometer exposure data over a 45-month period. Crashes were assigned to corridors by rider direction of travel, and rates were calculated per 100,000 vehicle kilometers traveled (VKT) citywide and by corridor. Across more than five million e-scooter kilometers of exposure, the citywide crash rate was 1.84 per 100,000 VKT, and 82.6% of crashes occurred at intersections or driveways. The 25 corridors accounted for 75.0% of crashes and 70.9% of VKT, with a combined rate (1.94 per 100,000 VKT) statistically indistinguishable from the rest of Nashville (1.58; p = 0.34). Corridor-level rates were nonetheless heterogeneous (chi-square = 96.17, df = 24, p < 0.001), with unadjusted rates ranging from 0.69 to 24.49 crashes per 100,000 VKT; empirical Bayes shrinkage reduced this spread to roughly 3.7-fold. Three corridors, Shelby Avenue, 21st Avenue, and West End Avenue, exceeded the citywide rate individually, with the first two remaining significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Exposure-adjusted corridor rates gave a different picture of risk than crash counts alone: citywide averages concealed substantial street-level variation, supporting corridor-level exposure measures as a screening tool for micromobility safety, though individual designations remain exploratory rather than confirmatory. These results let agencies combine trip and crash data to target safety investment at high-risk corridors.

As adaptive algorithms permeate professional settings, does higher algorithm adaptability enhance professional users’ usage intention? Drawing on Self-Determination Theory, three complementary studies were conducted: secondary analysis of Doubao AI-assistant reviews (N = 409), a between-subjects experiment with 190 participants simulating language-editing tasks, and a replication with 193 university faculty in authentic teaching contexts. Results showed that adaptability enhanced usage intention in subjective tasks but attenuated it in objective tasks. Mechanistically, higher adaptability promotes usage intention by strengthening users’ confidence in their ability to perform the task (task self-efficacy); however, in objective tasks it also erodes perceived transparency—a precondition for professionals to verify and take accountability for algorithmic outputs—thereby dampening usage intention. These opposing pathways jointly weaken the effect in objective tasks. This study extends algorithm-attitude theory by treating adaptability as an inherent design attribute, clarifying its dual pathways and boundary conditions, with practical implications for professional AI design.

Most virtual reality (VR) object-selection research restricts targets to the user’s initial field of view, thereby lacking ecological validity for omnidirectional applications. Addressing this limitation, our study investigates 360° object selection in VR, evaluating human performance, workload, and usability across varying postures (standing vs. seated) and steering strategies (physical body movement vs. controller). Through a human-subject experiment with 36 participants encompassing 24 azimuth and three inclination angles, we provide novel empirical evidence on full-surround target acquisition in VR. Results also reveal that physical body movement is faster and more usable when standing, while controller steering yields stable selection times across postures and reduces workload when seated. This finding suggests that optimal VR steering strategies are intrinsically linked to the user’s physical posture. Ultimately, this work advances our understanding of full-surround target acquisition in VR, contributing to empirical guidelines for designing adaptive, posture-aware spatial interaction techniques in omnidirectional virtual environments.

Elite strength and conditioning (S&C) coaches occupy a critical but underexamined position as first-line users of sports-science technology, responsible for translating raw athlete-monitoring data into immediate training decisions. Through seven semi-structured interviews with elite S & C coaches across NCAA Division I, professional, and Olympic contexts, we identify four recurring breakdowns in their daily data work: fragmented vendor ecosystems, metric overload, scale and staffing constraints and staff turnover. Static mockup elicitation during interviews revealed a consistent preference for simple, interpretable interfaces that foreground selected metrics and concise explanations over dense data displays. We position elite S&C coaches as a distinct user group whose needs are poorly served by current systems, and propose four design priorities: integration stability, selective metrics with contextual explanation, scale-aware views, and governance continuity, to guide future coach-facing sports-science interface design.

Abstract At unsignalized midblock crosswalks (UMCs), visual obstructions created by bike lane buffers can substantially affect drivers’ pedestrian detection and yielding behavior. However, limited evidence is available regarding how different types of bike lane buffers influence driving performance through changes in visual attention and cognitive workload. To address this issue, four representative bike lane buffer scenarios—Lawn, Railing, Bush, and Tree—were developed in a driving simulation environment. Vehicle operation parameters and eye-tracking data were collected simultaneously to investigate drivers’ behavioral and visual responses while approaching a crosswalk. The results showed that highly obstructive buffers significantly delayed pedestrian detection and weakened drivers’ early risk perception. In the Bush and Tree scenarios, pedestrians were detected at distances of only about 18 m from the crosswalk, representing a reduction of more than 40% compared with the low-obstruction conditions. As a consequence, drivers exhibited lower terminal braking speeds, higher maximum deceleration rates, and more abrupt braking maneuvers. The mean braking initiation distance in the Bush and Tree scenarios was approximately 48 m, which was more than 10 m shorter than that observed under the Lawn and Railing conditions. Eye-tracking analyses further revealed that highly obstructive environments significantly increased fixation duration on roadside areas while reducing the effective visual search range. In addition, the proportions of saccades and blinks decreased to approximately 3%, whereas the coefficient of variation of pupil diameter increased to 0.23, indicating elevated cognitive workload and mental stress. These findings demonstrate that visual obstructions associated with bike lane buffers can adversely affect drivers’ hazard perception, visual search behavior, and braking responses. The study provides empirical evidence to support the safety evaluation and design optimization of bike lane buffers near unsignalized midblock crosswalks.

Precise object manipulation in virtual reality (VR) remains challenging without haptic feedback. Haptic devices can improve motor performance but are often expensive, complex, and unsuitable for some tasks. We evaluate a composite pseudo-haptic configuration combining motion delay with realistic finger-object alignment to support precise object insertion. In a within-subject study, 25 participants grasped objects of different shapes and sizes and inserted them into matching holes. Compared with a default VR hand-grasp baseline, the pseudo-haptic configuration significantly reduced task completion times and collision durations with higher usability, lower workload, and higher presence. We performed a cross-study comparison between hardware-free and glove-based configurations using a prior haptic-glove study’s raw data with identical task structure, objects, and evaluation metrics. Results suggest the pseudo-haptic configuration achieved shorter task completion times and collision durations. Overall, the findings suggest that hardware-free pseudo-haptic configurations are promising for precise VR manipulation while reducing reliance on specialized haptic hardware.

Designing Knowledge Management Systems (KMSs) for higher education requires addressing complex human–technology interactions, especially where staff turnover and changing roles create challenges for reusing knowledge. While advances in process mining and Generative AI enable new ways of designing features to support knowledge management, existing KMSs often overlook the realities of educators' workflows, leading to low adoption and limited impact. This paper presents findings from a two-year human-centred design study with 108 higher education teachers, examining iterative co-design and evaluation of GoldMind – a KMS supporting in-the-flow knowledge management during digital teaching tasks. Through three design–evaluation cycles, we examined teachers' task-evaluations and how feedback informed refinements. Insights are synthesised across three themes: (1) Technology Lessons from user interaction data, (2) Design Considerations shaped by co-design and usability testing, and (3) Human Factors, including cognitive load and knowledge behaviours, analysed using Epistemic Network Analysis (in the last iteration). This study demonstrates that embedding human-centred, workflow-integrated KMSs can improve task efficiency, reduce cognitive load, and support knowledge reuse, while shaping educators' knowledge management behaviours through context-aware and proactive support. However, findings are based on a single-institution, controlled evaluation, limiting generalisability and requiring longitudinal, in-the-wild studies to assess adoption and impact.

This paper examines how community-led solidarity initiatives enable healing in the aftermath of disaster. Drawing on a two-year qualitative study in post-explosion Beirut, it explores how solidarity spaces function as relational structures of repair – sites where material response and affective recovery are not separate processes but mutually constitutive ones. While post-disaster organizing research has emphasized resource mobilization and agility, and disaster studies has identified the importance of community-led recovery, neither has fully explored how organizing enables healing to unfold collectively. Addressing this gap, the study makes two contributions. First, it reframes solidarity spaces as generative holding environments: relational infrastructures that simultaneously contain suffering and enable the emergence of new social arrangements. Second, it conceptualizes healing as organizing: a distributed, collective, and enacted process through which communities transform suffering into agency. Healing, in this account, is not an individual psychological process nor an outcome that follows organizing; it is the very practice through which recovery unfolds, as participants become agents of their own material and affective transformation through acts of solidarity.

Project-based learning (PjBL) is common in computing education, but traditional assessments of PjBL often fail to capture higher-order thinking (HOT), especially in transfer contexts. This study introduces ''design problems'' (DPs): concise, scenario-based prompts that require applying project concepts in new situations, to address this gap. We examined instructor perceptions, the ability of large language models (LLMs) to generate DPs, and student experiences. Surveys of 31 instructors, evaluation of 80 LLM-generated DPs, and student performance data showed that while instructors value DPs, creation effort is a barrier. LLMs helped by producing high-quality prompts with strong expert agreement. Students rated DPs from different LLMs similarly, and their performance on DP tasks showed negligible correlation with traditional project grades, suggesting DPs may capture distinct aspects of HOT. Keystroke data also suggested deeper cognitive engagement of students through planning and revision behaviors. Overall, DPs appear to be a useful complement to traditional assessments, especially in situations where AI use or collaboration may undermine individual learning.

Abstract Purpose : N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) is a polar aprotic solvent that is extensively used in the production of synthetic leather, polyurethane products, resins, adhesives and surface coatings. Potential sources of occupational exposures are mixing, formulation, coating, solvent transfer, cleaning, maintenance, and spill-response. DMF may be inhaled and absorbed through intact skin, which means that total internal dose for a particular worker may be underestimated by only measuring DMF in the air. Liver is a known target organ of DMF toxicity, and reports of increased liver enzymes and, less frequently, clinically significant liver injury have been reported in workers occupationally exposed to DMF. Increases in liver-function tests, however, are non-specific and can occur in people who drink too much alcohol and/or are obese, and/or may be caused by metabolic disease associated with steatotic liver disease, viral hepatitis, certain medicines (prescribed or not) or other exposures that may occur at work. Therefore, a comprehensive evaluation of possible liver damage from DMF should include exposure history, workplace monitoring, biological monitoring, repeated clinical evaluations, and the careful consideration of other causes of liver damage. Objective : The aim of this study is to find the relationship between DMF exposure and liver injury in the workers working in the synthetic leather, polyurethane, resin and surface-coating industries. It will consider exposure by inhalation and skin contact, estimate internal exposure as measured by urinary markers, review liver-function patterns as they change over time, determine if another source of liver injury or exposure may have occurred, and determine if a failure of workplace controls or medical surveillance could have led to exposure. The results will help to inform evidence-based occupational-health and medico-legal decisions about the possibility and level of occupational contribution to liver disease. Methods : An occupational-health study using a mixed-methods approach will be conducted with workers who may be at risk for DMF, such as mixers, formulators, coating operators, solvent-transfer workers, cleaners, maintenance workers, and waste-handling workers. A standardised occupational history will document job titles, length of employment, work patterns, frequency of tasks, use of DMF containing products, past chemical exposures, spillages, symptoms, hygiene practices and use and suitability of personal protective equipment (PPE). Task specific workplace exposure assessments will be carried out and personal air sampling will be used, wherever possible, especially during transfer, mixing, coating, cleaning and maintenance activities. The results of the air-monitoring will be evaluated against relevant occupational exposure concentrations with an understanding that an exposure below the airborne concentration limit does not mean there is no significant dermal absorption. The dermal exposure potential will be evaluated by conducting facility observations and interviews with workers, which will include direct hands-on contact with the material, use of contaminated gloves and clothing, gloves used, gloves replaced, local exhaust ventilation, housekeeping, spill control, washing facility, training, and working practices. The urinary concentrations of N-methylformamide (NMF) and N-acetyl-S-(N-methylcarbamoyl)cysteine (AMCC) will be measured for internal DMF exposure. These are markers of systemic exposure from all routes of exposure including inhalation and skin contact. Ideally, urine samples will be collected at the end of shift and end of work week, or at other suitable times depending on the toxicokinetic properties of the biomarker. Urine dilutions, e.g. creatinine, specific gravity etc., will be corrected and results interpreted taking into account the timing of the sample, the analytical procedure and available biological guidance values. Serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT), alkaline phosphatase (ALP) levels, bilirubin, albumin and international normalised ratio (INR) will be measured at regular intervals. These tests will assist in the identification of hepatocellular, cholestatic or mixed liver injury patterns and be useful in identifying transient, persistent or progressive liver injuries. Symptoms such as fatigue, nausea, abdominal discomfort, jaundice, pruritus and constitutional symptoms will also be recorded. Systematic assessment of potential confounding factors and alternative diagnosis. Alcohol intake, BMI, presence of diabetes, metabolic disease, pre-existing liver disease, other hepatotoxic chemicals and drug or supplement use will be recorded. Investigations may consist of a hepatology specialist review, abdominal ultrasound and hepatitis B and C testing, where clinically appropriate and consented to. There will be a structured medico-legal review, combining evidence from 4 domains – exposure, biological plausibility, individual clinical disease and duty of care. Occupational history and occupational monitoring will support the results of urinary biomarkers as evidence of internal exposure. The adequacy of engineering controls, local exhaust ventilation, training, spill management, hazard communication and medical surveillance will be taken into account in the duty of care assessment. Challenging with the drug after a possible hepatotoxic reaction will not take place. Expected Results : The study will not pre-judge causation as there is currently no data. It is anticipated to see if the workers with high overall or task specific exposure would have higher levels of urinary NMF and AMCC, and if these workers would have more frequent and persistent liver-test abnormalities. It will also be evaluated if liver enzymes improve if DMF exposure is reduced or eliminated, if follow up is available. Importantly, the analysis will differentiate isolated elevations of enzymes from a pattern of occupationally related disease. Conclusions :Concurring inhalational and dermal exposure to DMF is an occupational-health hazard that can be prevented. Task-based exposure assessment, urinary biomarkers, serial liver tests, clinical differential diagnosis and structured medico-legal analysis is a better approach for assessing possible occupational hepatotoxicity than liver enzymes alone. Decisions regarding the possibility, probability and highly probable occupational contribution will be based on the overall evidence and distinct from legal liability.PPE, training, spillage or medical surveillance had a significant impact on the workers.

documents.abstract: Near-miss events in the workplace serve as important signals for occupational accident prevention, and organizational responses to near-miss reports may influence employees’ perceived organizational support (POS). the association between organizational response patterns to near-miss reports and POS has not been sufficiently examined. This longitudinal study used data from an online cohort study of Japanese workers conducted at baseline (March 2023) and follow-up (December 2023). The analysis included 1,168 non-managerial workers who had experienced at least one near-miss event. Participants were categorized into four groups based on reporting behavior and the adequacy of organizational responses: reporting with adequate response, reporting with partial response, reporting with no response (reference), and no reporting. Associations between response patterns and POS at follow-up were examined using linear regression analysis. Employees in the reporting with adequate response (B = 2.16, 95% CI: 0.71–3.61) and reporting with partial response (B = 1.68, 95% CI: 0.12–3.23) groups showed significantly higher POS at follow-up compared with the reporting with no response group. The no reporting group also showed significantly higher POS (B = 1.63, 95% CI: 0.13–3.12). No significant moderating effect of company size was observed. These findings suggest that the quality of organizational responses to near-miss reports is associated with POS regardless of company size. Employees who reported near-miss events but received no organizational response showed the lowest POS, even lower than those who did not report. These findings highlight the importance of adequate follow-up and communication after near-miss reporting.

documents.abstract: Modern organizations often valorize speed and immediacy, treating acceleration as the dominant temporal logic of organizational life. Challenging this logic remains difficult, however, because organization studies lacks a well-developed conceptual language for alternative ways of engaging with time. We propose patience as one such alternative. Building on recent work on Eigenzeit, we argue that organizations can partially uncouple from external temporal pressures and develop forms of relative temporal autonomy that enable the orchestration of differentiated temporalities. While Eigenzeit highlights how organizations establish and sustain a temporality of their own amid complex temporal demands, less attention has been paid to the pacing through which this temporality is enacted in everyday organizational life. We therefore foreground pacing as the practical means by which organizations enact and sustain their own temporality. Within this context, patience emerges as a particular mode of pacing grounded in purposeful deceleration. To make this mode of pacing analytically visible, we identify four manifestations of organizational patience: waiting, restraining, forbearing, and persisting. Drawing on insights from the sociology of time, organization studies, and philosophy, we show how these manifestations represent distinct ways of pacing organizational activities by holding time open, delaying intervention, staying with difficulty, and sustaining engagement over time. By reframing patience as a distinctive mode of pacing rather than passive inactivity, we show how organizations cultivate and sustain an Eigenzeit through practices that contribute to the orchestration of competing temporal demands. This perspective advances organization studies by illuminating how temporal orchestration is accomplished through everyday organizational interactions and how patience enables organizations to sustain resilience and meaningful engagement in the face of acceleration pressures.

Passenger-facing vehicle interfaces must inform without disrupting non-driving activities. This study related HMI communication during fully automated driving to passenger physiology and interaction quality during concurrent reading. Twenty-six participants completed a no-communication Baseline drive and one HMI drive with abstract auditory-tactile cues (Simple) or synthesised speech (Extended); 24 contributed physiological data. Electrodermal activity (EDA) was the primary measure, with User Experience Questionnaire ratings. Because HMI variant was assigned between participants, participant-level analyses provided primary condition inference. Mean EDA was lower in both HMI conditions than Baseline, but no contrast was statistically supported (Simple–Baseline −73.1, 95% CI [−160.3, 14.0], p = 0.092; Extended–Baseline −44.7, p = 0.296; Extended–Simple 28.4, p = 0.614). No UEQ scale survived multiplicity correction. Segment-level mixed-effects models (803 segments) reproduced this ordering with narrower intervals reflecting repeated observations, not independent assignments. Participant-level contrasts matched the unit of assignment; segment-level models characterised temporal physiological variation.

Abstract Background Ergonomics is an often-overlooked component of operative education. Early intervention can protect residents from physical stress and long-term musculoskeletal injury. Our aim is to evaluate residents during a simulated suturing exercise and assess the impact of self-evaluation on ergonomics. Methods Following informed consent, surgical residents performed a simulated complex wound closure, blinded to the study’s focus. Following initial closure, residents reviewed their videos with an ergonomic self-assessment guide, repeated the exercise, and completed a post-survey. Representative video clips were analyzed to measure elbow, spine, and neck angles. Standard angles were defined as 90–110° for elbow, < 10° for spine, and < 25° for neck. Results Twenty residents participated across four post-graduate years (PGY): five PGY-4, four PGY-3, four PGY-2, and seven PGY-1. Across all participants, we found significant reduction in spine (12.5° vs 5.1°, p = 0.016) and neck (58.5° vs 46.4°, p = 0.004) angle during the second exercise, but no difference in elbow angle (102.7° vs 101.7°, p = 0.744). The post-survey revealed most residents think about their ergonomics in the operating room at least weekly (75%) and feel physical strain (95%). All residents (100%) reported improved awareness of ergonomics and perceived transferability to the clinical setting. Discussion Our study demonstrated a resident self-assessment of ergonomics led to significant improvement in spinal and neck angles in a simulated exercise with increased awareness of operative ergonomics and perceived transferability to the clinical setting. These findings support integration of ergonomic education early in surgical training to help reduce physical strain and promote operative longevity.

Nearly hundred studies in different times and places have documented that self-employed people report higher levels of subjective well-being than employed people. This “entrepreneurship well-being premium” is typically interpreted causally—"being your own boss" enhances well-being via more autonomy, favorable work design, and basic psychological need fulfillment. Yet, most of the evidence so far is cross-sectional, explanations fragmented across different theoretical mechanisms while rigorous tests distinguishing causation from selection are rather rare. We address this gap by first mapping five theoretical mechanisms—(1) procedural utility, (2) job demands-resources, (3) self-determination, (4) person–environment fit, and (5) selection on stable traits—into distinct stages of the causal process, further deriving discriminating predictions about each mechanism. In turn, using three waves of the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) survey and two waves from the Global Flourishing study, we evaluate these competing predictions with a battery of converging tests, including cross-section analyses, individual fixed-effects models, and pre-transition analyses.

In this paper, we examine how incumbent-led mobilization against Uber’s platform entry in Europe relates to regulatory bans, public attention, and consumer-side uptake. Combining hand-coded data on taxi-sector tactics and frames with first regulatory bans, Uber app downloads, and Google search interest across 22 European countries from 2012 to 2020, we identify a differentiated temporal pattern. Private tactics are strongly associated with first-ban hazard in the short window following mobilization, whereas lawsuits are positively associated over a longer window. The frames incumbents deploy also matter: legitimacy-challenge frames portraying UberPop as incompatible with lawful and fair competition are more consistently associated with bans than compliance-dispute frames focused on tax or labor obligations. At the same time, private tactics and lawsuits coincide with immediate increases in app downloads and Google search interest, indicating an attention spillover from incumbent contestation. Lawsuit-related download elevations display marginally greater persistence than those associated with private tactics, although this difference is not stronger early after entry. Taken together, the findings show that incumbent mobilization in platform markets can be associated with regulatory bans and consumer-side uptake of the entrants they seek to exclude at the same time. The results establish temporal association, although the direction of influence within this process cannot be isolated.

Avoiding loss-of-control events will be key to industry and society as AI technology is employed in various critical processes. In this article, we assess a hypothetical instability situation of an AGI − a singularity event − from a safety science standpoint. We present one way to describe the process of how a real time Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) in its interaction with the environment may set it in a runaway condition. Our goal is clarifying general and structural control issues of strong real time AI for design, safeguarding and legislation. In cybernetics, instability and hence, the risk of loss-of-control, is a core trait of all highly adaptive systems. Such adaptive behavior can manifest as radical reframing – a pivotal process of a system that enables it to solve very hard challenges, and which requires it to redefine its core concepts, goals, values, plans and procedures. What emerges is the AGI power dilemma ; a double-bind between performance and controllability of a real time system. We discuss the consequences for human control of AGI and prospects for safeguarding when optimizing for power and speed. Moreover, we conclude that the human in the loop approach gives an illusion of safety when the AI is optimized for power.

documents.abstract: A persistent puzzle in human-computer interaction (HCI) is that AI training often fails to improve performance in AI-assisted tasks. This study introduces AI Metacognitive Calibration (AIMC), capturing users’ self-reported monitoring and adaptive regulation of cognitive engagement with AI systems. Using a sequential mixed-methods design (interviews with 24 knowledge workers followed by a survey of 289 professionals), we develop and validate the AIMC scale. Confirmatory factor analysis confirmed three first-order reflective dimensions: Monitoring Awareness (MA), Critical Evaluation (CE), and Adaptive Regulation (AR). Polynomial regression revealed a pattern consistent with an inverted-U association between AIMC and human–AI collaborative performance (HAICP), with performance peaking at moderate AIMC levels. Task complexity and AI system transparency moderated the location of the performance peak. Users with insufficient AIMC over-rely on AI output; users with excessive AIMC incur metacognitive overload. Findings challenge the “more training is better” assumption and reframe AI interface design toward calibration support.

The ubiquity of media multitasking and its negative effects on task performance underscore the importance of understanding what drives this behavior. While theoretical models propose that media multitasking arises from an interplay between individual trait and contextual factors, little research has directly examined it from this perspective. Across two studies, we explored the joint role of these factors in media multitasking. Study 1 examined whether relations between in-study media multitasking and individual traits in attention, self-regulation, and real-world media multitasking tendencies differed based on the contextual variable of task difficulty. Individual trait and contextual factors interacted when predicting media multitasking; however, results may have been affected by engagement with activities unrelated to the experimental content. Study 2 investigated the stability of multitasking behaviors and their associations with individual traits across two timepoints. Media multitasking was moderately correlated across sessions and did not consistently correlate with individual traits. It was, however, associated with greater enjoyment of the secondary media. Our findings suggest that media multitasking and its relations with trait measures are highly context-dependent, such that researchers studying media multitasking should carefully consider its sensitivity to context.

documents.abstract: Steering through width-changing paths is fundamental in graphical user interface (GUI) tasks such as lasso selection. Researchers in ergonomics have modelled movement times by path shape, but most studies examined only linear width changes. We investigated the generalisability of the Steering Law by measuring movement times in paths where the width changes according to exponential, quadratic, and sigmoid functions. The global steering model yielded R-squared values ranging from 0.9304 to 0.9934, but for quadratic paths, a model that approximated the width change as linear showed improved goodness-of-fit indices. This is presumably because, according to speed profile and cursor trajectory analyses, participants were unable to effectively utilise the bulging part of the path for acceleration. Our work helps to clarify the behaviours in GUI operations and also offers the possibility of model simplification in applications using the Steering Law, such as difficulty setting in racing video games.

Generative AI is used through natural-language prompting, yet few validated measures test whether self-assessed prompting competence matches demonstrated skill. We developed the Prompt Engineering Expertise Battery (PEEB), a 29-item self-report scale and a five-task performance module organized around seven dimensions. In Phase 1 (N = 257), internal consistency was high (α = 0.97), but exploratory parallel analysis retained a single factor, which replicated across random split halves; the scale is therefore scored as one total, captured by a 14-item short form (α = 0.95). In Phase 2, 60 participants completed screen-shared tasks scored by three raters (ICC(2,k) = 0.94). Self-report related only weakly to performance (r = 0.18, 95% CI [−0.07, 0.42]), a preliminary estimate; prompts were brief and disclosed sensitive information in 71% of health tasks. Assessments of prompting competence should include task-based measures, and the structure, short form, and performance module need confirmation in an independent sample.

documents.abstract: Signed PDF documents have legally binding value under frameworks such as the EU's eIDAS regulation. In this work, we present Genuine PDF Forgeries, a novel attack class that focuses on human factors in signature validation. Our attacks target the disconnect between cryptographically verifiable signer certificates and human-visible signature blocks embedded in documents. We analyze our attacks against 23 PDF viewers and validation tools across desktop platforms and the web. We find that nine of the 13 viewers that automatically report signature validity hide authenticated signer information behind additional user interaction. We then evaluate the attack in twin deception-based online studies with 584 EU-based participants. To further validate the impact, we perform a highly tailored real-world attack study with six trials within two privacy-sensitive organizations. Five of six organizational trials accepted requests authenticated using the forged visual identity. In the online studies (total n=584), the most effective attack variant deceives 71.9% of eligible participants on first impression, and 57.3% continue to be deceived even after we prompt for additional introspection. We derive viewer-side countermeasures and prototype a safeguard that overlays the untrusted signature block with signer information obtained from the validated certificate. Our results show that boolean validity indicators, not associated with the authenticated signer identity, are insufficient in practice.

Generative AI is increasingly used to support interpersonal communication, yet little is known about how user-visible rationales shape users’ evaluations of AI-assisted messages. We examine this question in Chinese family group chats, where correcting older relatives’ health misinformation requires factual accuracy alongside care, respect, and face management. In a between-subjects experiment (N = 279), participants viewed the same corrective reply preceded by no visible rationale, a procedural rationale, or a relational rationale. Both rationale conditions increased performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and adoption intention while reducing AI-mediated authenticity concern. Relational rationale produced the largest reduction in authenticity concern, and its effect on performance expectancy strengthened as affective load increased. Overall, user-visible rationales appear to function as communicative frames that shape how users evaluate AI-assisted interpersonal messages, extending research on explainable AI and AI-mediated communication.

Abstract Background Electronic personal health record (PHR) systems allow individuals to access and manage their medical records seamlessly across healthcare providers to enhance service delivery and health outcomes. The success of the PHR systems depends on people’s willingness to use (WTU) them. Despite the increasing implementation of this technology in Malaysia, there is a lack of official documentation regarding its acceptance or adoption. Given its high implementation costs, it is essential to gauge the public’s WTU, assess the findings, and take appropriate measures to improve it. Methods This study aimed to determine the WTU as well as understand its predictors and insights among multi-ethnic civil servants from 15 ministries in Putrajaya, Malaysia, using a convergent mixed-methods study. The cross-sectional study was based on the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology with linear regression analysis. Meanwhile, the generic qualitative study was based on semi-structured interviews with thematic analysis. Results The majority of respondents were willing to use the PHR system both currently and in the future. Significant predictors of performance expectancy (PE), facilitating conditions (FC), and social influence (SI) were integrated with the six themes of PE, FC, SI, effort expectancy (EE), human factors (HF), and perceived risk (PR). PE influenced WTU through health status, convenience, administrative efficiency, and incentives, while FC encompassed accessibility, self-efficacy, and assistance. SI depended on the impact of the healthcare provider, social connections, social media figure, promotion, stranger, and sense of autonomy. As for EE, informants underscored the importance of system integration, stability, and user interface. Additionally, HF extended beyond age, gender, and experience to include race, education, income, and employment. Meanwhile, PR was in regard to security, privacy, information credibility, and legal instruments. Conclusion Addressing these domains through tailored strategies can fulfil population needs, enhance system optimization, increase user acceptance, and support sustainable nationwide PHR system adoption.

This repository provides materials from a professional development programme at Universidad Tecnológica Israel, Ecuador, on designing instruction around authentic professional tasks using the Four-Component Instructional Design (4C/ID) model. The programme helps university teachers connect syllabus learning outcomes with the integrated knowledge, skills and attitudes required for professional performance. The materials combine explanatory guides, worked design examples, classroom modelling, participant assignments and design worksheets. A continuing example (i.e., conducting a critical literature review to substantiate the preliminary definition of an educational research problem) illustrates how the design decisions connect across sessions. Participants apply the same principles to tasks from their own disciplines. The materials are shared to document the training and support scholarly discussion, reuse and adaptation in higher education. They describe the programme’s instructional rationale and activities; they do not report an empirical evaluation of its effectiveness.

As autonomous vehicles (AVs) become integrated into everyday transportation, developing accurate mental models of automated systems is essential for safe and effective human–vehicle interaction. Inspired by using pre-flight briefings in the aviation industry, this study examined participants’ perceptions of training across the Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) levels of driving automation. Fifty-one U.S.-based participants were surveyed about their understandings of AV systems, their reliance behaviors on them, and preferences for training across five SAE levels. Our data revealed that most participants preferred receiving some form of training across all levels of automation. Individuals’ personal preferences for mandatory training increased with higher levels of automation and were strongly aligned with their beliefs on legally required training. Additionally, accessible onboarding approaches, particularly in-vehicle tutorials, were identified as the most preferred training format. Overall, our findings highlight the importance of supporting mental model formation to facilitate safe and effective use of AVs.

There is growing recognition of the importance of designing work environments that promote the well-being of diverse employees. Although the Job Demands–Resources (JD–R) model has contributed substantially to work engagement research, there remains scope to extend it to address the challenge of creating inclusive work environments. We examined the associations of workplace tolerance and individual autonomy with work engagement, including the potential mediating roles of psychological safety and intrinsic motivation. We used data from 1084 Japanese workers collected across four waves of online surveys and conducted causal mediation analyses. As a result, the presence of tolerant coworkers was associated with work engagement through workplace psychological safety (total effect = 0.296; proportion mediated = 29.7 %), whereas the absence of intolerant coworkers was not clearly associated with work engagement. Individual autonomy was also associated with work engagement through intrinsic motivation (total effect = 0.444), although the proportion mediated was modest (14.5 %). These findings suggest that positioning workplace tolerance and individual autonomy as social and personal resources, respectively, may extend the JD–R model by enabling it to describe the conditions under which employees with diverse characteristics and circumstances can engage in their work on an equitable basis.

This study examined associations between propensity to trust automation (PTT) and 27 other personal characteristic dimensions across 11 constructs: cultural values, attentional control, mood, personality, risk propensity, decision-making style, reasoning, negative attitudes, expectancy, self-efficacy, and the perfect automation schema. A total of 166 participants completed pre-experiment surveys before working with automated drone teammates in a simulated threat-detection task. PTT correlated most strongly with performance expectancy ( r = .46), effort expectancy ( r = .30), negative attitudes toward interacting with autonomous systems ( r = −.28), and the high expectations subscale of the perfect automation schema ( r = .24). Smaller but significant correlations were observed for intellect, masculinity, power distance, and risk propensity. PTT also correlated significantly with post-experiment trust and satisfaction. These results suggest that PTT is associated primarily with expectations about automation and negative attitudes toward interacting with it, and only secondarily with broader personal characteristics.

Understanding users’ experiences with authentication is key to developing usable and secure systems, especially in contexts where security risks are high. We conduct a survey and time-diary study ( N = 21) at a large public university to understand the timing and overhead of daily authentication activities across devices and settings. Our findings reveal that people are required to authenticate three times more often than a decade ago (an average of 76 times per day), with an average authentication time overhead of 13.9 min per day. The majority (90.5%) of participants reported frustration with authentication, and 61.9% reported at least one problematic authentication experience that increased their daily temporal and cognitive overhead.

The rapid digitalisation of financial services has increased individuals’ exposure to online fraud. However, recent literature highlights that identifying a clear profile of fraud victims remains challenging, as individual-level factors examined so far do not fully explain fraud vulnerability. This study examines how financial literacy, digital financial literacy, and financial graph literacy are associated with individuals’ susceptibility to fraud. Moving beyond aggregate measures, the study adopts a multidimensional framework that distinguishes, for both financial and digital financial literacy, between knowledge, attitudes, and behavior, and introduces financial graph literacy as a key capability for interpreting visually presented financial information. The study combines survey-based measures with an embedded experimental task and employs regression and mediation analyses. The findings show that financial and digital financial knowledge are not consistently associated with lower fraud victimization. Higher financial and digital financial attitude scores are associated with lower fraud victimization, whereas higher scores on the financial behavior index are associated with greater reported victimization. Financial graph literacy is also associated with lower fraud victimization. Indirect-effect estimates are consistent with partial mediation through overconfidence for digital financial attitude and financial graph literacy. Financial graph literacy is also associated with lower end-anchoring, i.e. a disproportionate reliance on the final movement of a stock-price graph, but end-anchoring is not associated with fraud victimization. Overall, the study advances a process-oriented and behaviorally grounded understanding of fraud vulnerability, emphasizing the interplay among literacy components and cognitive biases.

Human decision-making is often influenced by cognitive biases, especially under uncertainty and risk. Prior works have studied biases in single-step decision environments with immediate outcomes or in interaction with a single AI agent. However, less attention has been given to (1) cascaded settings with delayed outcomes, where decision at one step influences future system states and (2) to interaction with multiple AI agents. To study this, we designed a naval battle strategy game where participants interact with two AI advisors. We find asymmetric responses to positive and negative outcomes, with significant changes after negative outcomes. Participants failed to identify the actions responsible for failures and misattributed responsibility across AI agents, leading them to modify decisions steps weakly related to the true cause of poor performance. We refer to this behavior as bias in error attribution. Our findings show how cognitive biases can emerge in human-multi AI teams in cascaded settings.

Abstract Background: Ensuring a sustainable nursing workforce requires both academic capacity building and a deeper understanding of the experiences that nurture students’ commitment to the profession. In India, rapid growth in nursing education has intersected with changing societal perceptions and competitive career landscapes. This study sought to explore career choice motivations, professional perceptions, and future career intentions among Indian nursing students. Methods: A sequential explanatory mixed-methods approach was gently conducted between April 2025 and June 2026. Phase I involved an online cross-sectional survey (N=1544) across multiple geographical zones. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the data. Group comparison tests, and multiple linear regression modelling were also used. Phase II comprised semi-structured qualitative interviews (N=27) analyzed using Colaizzi’s descriptive phenomenological approach to better contextualize the statistical findings. Quantitative and qualitative strands were integrated via joint display and narrative synthesis. Results: A notable proportion of participants (69.8%) reported considering alternative career choices, most commonly medicine (37.4%) and technical fields (25.8%). Mean domain scores indicated high intrinsic motivation (19.94 ± 4.61) and economic expectations (20.00 ± 4.11), alongside academic stress (20.03 ± 3.90). Multiple regression analysis (F = 5.085, p < 0.001, R² = 0.103) showed that female gender (B = 4.717, p < 0.001) and salary expectations (B = 1.493, p = 0.002) were positively associated with perception scores, whereas career change intention (B = −4.659, p < 0.001) and higher secondary examination marks (B = −1.905, p = 0.002) were negatively associated. Qualitative findings, organized into seven themes and 27 subthemes, provided explanatory context. Students described how entrance exam setbacks, heavy assignment loads, inconsistent mentorship, and social stigma contributed to uncertainty. In contrast, rewarding patient encounters and the development of clinical confidence fostered a growing sense of professional commitment. Conclusion: Indian nursing students navigate diverse pathways into the profession, balancing altruistic goals with practical challenges and evolving career preferences. The results tentatively highlight that supportive career counseling, refined academic requirements, enhanced clinical mentorship, and clear role definitions may help strengthen students' professional identity and support long-term commitment to nursing practice.

Standard pediatric cognitive and projective assessments can be monotonous and provoke anxiety. This reduces children's engagement and compliance and diminishes the quality of observable behavior. In this work, we present a workflow that transfers routine paper-and-pencil tasks to a tablet application and adds a NAO humanoid robot as a social partner. Our goal is to provide a robot-and-tablet system for standardized assessments. In this exploratory study, we focused on quantifying the added contribution of the robot to engagement compared to a tablet-only system. To this end, we evaluated the workflow in a pediatric clinic with 24 participants, each with a distinct neurodevelopmental disorder diagnosis, using a controlled, between-subjects design. The tablet-only condition delivered the same activities and pacing without robot cues. This served as a control to isolate the effect of social scaffolding. Licensed therapists rated engagement using the Pediatric Assessment of Rehabilitation Engagement (PARE) scale. Our preliminary findings suggest that the robot's presence supported higher observable engagement and sustained participation without altering the rapport within the child–therapist–robot triad. Moreover, results in the PARE scale were significantly different between the two conditions when considering the age of the little patients (with mean age 10 vs. 8, respectively). While the small sample size and age distribution warrant cautious interpretation, this work highlights a robot's potential contribution to children's engagement during standardized assessment.

Cognitive friction has been described both as productive resistance intended to sustain cognitive engagement and as effort required to overcome obstacles in AI interaction. These uses create uncertainty about the boundaries of the construct and the mechanisms attributed to it across different contexts. To clarify how cognitive friction is defined and distinguished from related constructs, and to map the mechanisms described as generating it across educational, professional, and everyday human–AI interactions. English-language empirical and non-empirical sources will be eligible where they provide substantive conceptual or mechanistic content relevant to cognitive friction or potentially related constructs in human–AI interaction. Eligible evidence may include journal articles, conference papers, theses, substantive commentaries, and full preprints or working papers. Electronic searches were conducted on 22 October 2026 in Scopus, APA PsycInfo, Web of Science Core Collection, ERIC, arXiv and SSRN. Backward and forward citation searching will supplement these searches. Two reviewers will independently screen records and assess full texts against predefined eligibility criteria. Two reviewers will independently chart data using a structured Google Sheets workbook. Data will be analysed through descriptive mapping and basic qualitative content analysis. No formal critical appraisal or risk-of-bias assessment will be conducted.

The growing integration of cyber, physical, and operational security functions has created a need for assessment approaches that evaluate security convergence as an organisational capability rather than as a set of isolated controls. This article proposes the Converged Security Maturity Index (CSMI), a conceptual maturity model designed to assess the level of integration among cybersecurity, physical security, and operational security within organisations. The model is developed using a design science research approach grounded in a structured review of converged security literature, cyber–physical system security, and existing maturity frameworks. CSMI comprises five progressive maturity levels—Fragmented, Coordinated, Integrated, Unified, and Optimised—and evaluates organisational capabilities across four dimensions: governance and strategy, processes and incident management, technology and infrastructure integration, and human factors and organisational culture. The article describes the architecture of the model and the rationale for each maturity level and dimension and outlines how the framework could be applied in practice through a structured questionnaire in future work. The proposed framework aims to support organisational self-assessment, benchmarking, and identification of convergence gaps across different sectors.

Cybersickness remains a barrier to immersive virtual reality adoption. This systematic review and exploratory meta-analysis synthesized mitigation studies using head-mounted displays. Six databases were searched for peer-reviewed studies published during 2014–2025 that compared mitigation with a control using standardized sickness outcomes. Risk of bias was assessed using design-appropriate tools. Fifty-nine studies were classified into seven categories; 39 (66%) reported at least one significant reduction. Exploratory random-effects analyses yielded pooled effects for field-of-view restriction (k = 6, g = 0.48) and heterogeneous cognitive/behavioral interventions (k = 3, g = 0.79, I² = 56%). Five of 13 studies using both the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire and Fast Motion Sickness Scale found significant effects only on the latter. No study had low overall risk of bias, and only two reported preregistration. Two provisional frameworks, the Multi-Level Cybersickness Modulation model and Temporal Dynamics Framework, are proposed to generate testable hypotheses and require prospective validation.

Understanding cognitive biases in cyber attacker behavior can help develop countermeasures that leverage predictable mental shortcuts. This paper analyzes the impact of one such bias, the default effect, on cyber attack decisions. Three forms of this effect are examined: explicit default, association effect, and position effect. The experiment included 85 participants who displayed cybersecurity knowledge based on a screening assessment. The participants performed established behavioral tasks and cyber-adapted scenarios involving host selection, port selection, and password spraying. Our findings confirmed that explicit defaults behave as expected from prior research: people preferred the default option more often under opt-out than opt-in framing. For cyber tasks, the association effect was always present and influential as participants preferred options semantically related to the contextual cues provided. In contrast, position effects failed to emerge when semantically meaningful cues were available. Results offer actionable insights for designing cyber defense systems that leverage predictable attacker heuristics.

To safely and efficiently manage increasing drone traffic, Uncrewed Air Traffic Management (UTM) is currently being developed with high levels of automation. In low-altitude airspace around airports, human supervision remains essential to ensure safe separation between drones and crewed aircraft, requiring transparency to support oversight of automated decision-making. Although transparency has been shown to improve understanding, trust, and performance, relatively little is known about transparency-seeking behavior during real-time supervision. This article presents a novel on-demand interface for tactical UTM, comprising eight information overlays derived from a consolidated transparency taxonomy that unifies previously fragmented transparency constructs. A human-in-the-loop experiment with 16 participants investigated transparency usage under varying traffic conditions, automation failures, and two autonomous path-planning algorithms: the graph-based Zeta*-SIPP and the sampling-based Informed RRT*. The results show that information about the Closest Point of Approach between drones and crewed aircraft was operationally most valuable. During automation failures, participants increasingly requested information about changes in constraints and traffic situations, together with the planner’s internal reasoning, to diagnose failures and guide intervention decisions. Furthermore, the sampling-based planner revealed an important boundary condition for transparency research: the cognitive costs and benefits of algorithmic transparency during real-time supervision depend on the characteristics of the underlying algorithm and how its search process is presented. Overall, this study shows that transparency requirements are dynamic, depending on user needs, operational context, and the underlying autonomy, and that complementary transparency perspectives can be successfully integrated into a single adaptable interface.

Abstract Runway overruns rank among the most frequent and economically significant accident categories in commercial aviation, typically arising from the nonlinear combination of performance variabilities during the approach and landing phases. Existing risk models either rely on historical accident databases or treat runway overrun precursors as independent binary events, overlooking the interactive dynamics of everyday flight operations. This paper introduces FRAM-FDM, a quantitative methodology that integrates the Functional Resonance Analysis Method (FRAM) with Flight Data Monitoring (FDM) to assess and manage operational runway overrun risk from a Safety-II perspective. The methodology deconstructs the approach-and-landing sociotechnical system into functional couplings, quantifies their output variabilities using real flight data recorder (FDR) data, and aggregates them through: (i) linear regression combined with Monte Carlo Simulation (MCS) for probabilistic fleet-level risk estimation; (ii) logistic regression with odds-ratio analysis to rank precursor influence; and (iii) metadata-driven scenario simulation in the FRAM Model Visualiser (FMV). Applied to a case study of 110 landings — including one overrun event — from a business jet fleet, the framework identifies airspeed excess at the runway threshold and brake application profile as the dominant risk contributors, demonstrates synergistic risk amplification when multiple variabilities co-occur, and provides actionable guidance for training and procedure reinforcement. FRAM-FDM advances FRAM toward a fully quantitative, data-driven implementation and aligns FDM programmes with Safety-II principles.

Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly used by medical students for academic purposes, yet how patterns of such use relate to academic motivation and self-efficacy remain insufficiently characterized, particularly in the Iranian medical education context. This study examined the frequency and purpose of AI tool use among medical students and their associations with academic motivation and academic self-efficacy. Methods A descriptive-analytical cross-sectional study was conducted among medical students at Kashan University of Medical Sciences, Iran, in 2026. Using proportionate stratified sampling across four educational stages, 111 students completed a questionnaire package comprising a researcher-developed AI-use instrument (separate frequency and purpose scores), the Persian Academic Motivation Scale, and the Persian College Academic Self-Efficacy Scale. Associations between the two AI-use scores and five outcomes (self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, amotivation, and composite positive motivation) were examined using Spearman correlation with Bonferroni correction, followed by five multiple linear regression models adjusting for age, sex, educational stage, and GPA. Results Conversational AI tools, most notably ChatGPT, were used by nearly all participants. Both AI-use frequency and purpose were positively correlated with academic self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and positive motivation, and negatively correlated with amotivation (Spearman ρ = 0.46–0.77; all p < 0.001, surviving Bonferroni correction). In adjusted models, AI-use purpose remained independently associated with all five outcomes (standardized β = 0.32–0.69), whereas AI-use frequency remained independently associated only with self-efficacy (β = 0.55, p < 0.001). GPA was independently associated with intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and positive motivation, but not self-efficacy or amotivation. No significant differences by sex or educational stage were observed. The five models explained 40% to 61% of outcome variance. Conclusions The purpose for which medical students use AI tools showed more consistent independent associations with academic motivation and self-efficacy than frequency of use alone, suggesting that how AI is used may be more relevant to these outcomes than how often it is used. As an observational, cross-sectional study, these findings describe association rather than causal sequence, and contribute context-specific evidence on AI use and its psychological correlates among medical students in Iran.
